entry.title: SAP Dynamic Forms 2606 Now Available – What's New?
entry.content:
The 2606 release of SAP Dynamic Forms brings meaningful advances across AI-driven automation, offline field capabilities, geographic availability, form governance, and deeper integration with SAP maintenance processes. From migrating legacy PDF forms automatically to expanding the platform to new Google Cloud Platform regions, this release helps organizations modernize faster and work more flexibly — wherever their teams operate.

Key highlights include AI-assisted form migration, fully offline support for form images and attachments, new GCP data center regions, a Form Builder view mode, a new timestamp control, enhanced notifications from form data, mass assignment of form definitions, and additional usability improvements.

AI-Assisted Form Migration

One of the most impactful enhancements in 2606 is AI-assisted form migration, which enables organizations to convert existing PDF forms into SAP Dynamic Forms definitions automatically — eliminating the need for manual recreation and significantly reducing setup time.

Using generative AI, the capability interprets the structure and content of an existing PDF form and generates the corresponding SAP Dynamic Forms definition, including fields, controls, sections, and grids, as well as key metadata. Users can then review, refine, and deploy the migrated form with minimal effort.

This dramatically lowers the barrier to adoption for organizations with large catalogs of paper or PDF-based forms, helping them modernize their processes faster and with less manual overhead.

Offline Support for Form Images and Attachments

Field workers frequently capture photos and attach files while completing forms in locations with limited or no connectivity. With the 2606 release, form instances downloaded to SAP Service and Asset Manager (SSAM) devices now also download all previously attached files and images — making the full form experience, including attachments, available offline.

All attachments can be opened directly on the device in the offline client. This release also adds support for SSAM's 'supervisor mode,' ensuring that reassigned forms can be reviewed with their attachments intact — even without a connection.

This enhancement is essential for organizations in industries such as utilities, manufacturing, and oil and gas, where technicians and inspectors frequently work in remote or connectivity-challenged environments.

 

Google Cloud Platform Data Center Expansion

The 2606 release extends the geographic availability of SAP Dynamic Forms with support for Google Cloud Platform (GCP) data centers, enabling customers in additional regions to deploy the solution closer to their operations. The following data centers are now supported:

  • cf-ap30 – Australia (Sydney)
  • cf-br30 – Brazil (São Paulo)
  • cf-eu30 – Europe (Frankfurt)
  • cf-jp30 – Japan (Osaka)
  • cf-sa30 – KSA (Dammam)
  • cf-sa31 – KSA (Dammam)
  • cf-us30 – US Central (IA)
  • cf-us31 – US Central (IA)*
  • cf-ap31 – Singapore**
  • cf-eu31 – Europe (Netherlands)**

Note: *cf-us31 is planned for SAP Dynamic Forms 2609. **cf-ap31 and cf-eu31 are planned for SAP Dynamic Forms 2612.

 

Form Builder View Mode (Read-Only Permissions)

The 2606 release introduces a view mode in Form Builder, adding support for read-only permissions on form definitions. This allows organizations to grant users visibility into form designs without enabling them to make changes — supporting review, audit, and governance scenarios where access control over form authoring is important.

New Timestamp Control with Time Zone Support

SAP Dynamic Forms 2606 introduces a new timestamp control that supports both device and browser time zones. This ensures that date and time values captured in forms are accurately recorded relative to the local context of the user completing the form — whether they are working on a mobile device in the field or using a browser in the office. This is particularly valuable for organizations operating across multiple time zones or geographies.

 

 

Enhanced Support for Creating Notifications from Forms

SAP Dynamic Forms 2606 expands the capability to create maintenance notifications directly from form data, reducing duplicate data entry and accelerating defect and issue reporting. This release adds support for three additional data types:

  • Long Text: Long text fields from forms can now be mapped to the notification long text, enabling richer defect descriptions to flow directly into SAP maintenance records.
  • GPS Point → GEF: GPS coordinates captured in forms can be transferred to the Geographic Enhancement Framework (GEF), supporting location-based maintenance and asset tracking.
  • Form Attachments → DMS: Attachments included in a form can be transferred to the Document Management System (DMS) as part of the notification creation process, keeping supporting evidence linked to the maintenance record.

Mass Assignment of Form Definitions to Task List Headers and Operations

The 2606 release introduces the ability to mass-assign form definitions to task list headers and operations, making it significantly easier to roll out forms at scale. Rather than assigning forms individually, administrators can now apply form definitions across multiple task list items in a single action, reducing administrative effort and accelerating deployment for organizations with large or complex maintenance task structures.

Additional Enhancements

The 2606 release also includes the following usability improvements:

  • Multi-Column Sorting: Sorting across multiple columns is now supported in Form Builder, Form Runner, and Administrator details lists, improving navigation and data management for users working with large volumes of form data.
  • Form Runner Status Display: Form status is now more prominently visible in Form Runner, helping users quickly understand the state of their forms at a glance.

Summary

The 2606 release of SAP Dynamic Forms brings together advances in AI automation, offline field capabilities, platform availability, and maintenance integration. These enhancements help organizations deploy forms faster, support field teams more effectively, and connect form-based workflows more tightly with their core SAP maintenance processes.

SAP Dynamic Forms

entry.title: Re: Production Orders creates many Materials out of one
entry.content:
Hi @sergio_perdomo you really need to get your requirements straight. Initially you said you have multiple semi-finished product after cutting. Now, you said you have one semi-finished. Which is right then?

  1. If you have only one, then there is not a problem, it is a regular process.
  2. If you physically have multiple semi-finished, but you always keep them together, consume together and ship together, then you can manage them all with a single material number.
  3. If you physically have multiple semi-finished and they are independent, i.e. can be consumed or shipped separately, then you need to manage each of them under a separate material number.

I don't see any other reasonable option. You can try to merge somehow option 3 with 2 and manage independent semi-finished with a single material number, but it is a surefire recipe for disaster.

entry.title: Re: SAP PP/ABAP: Recursive BOM Explosion for Cross-Plant...
entry.content:
Hi Sanket,

Before writing the recursion, I would check the special procurement type behind the key, because the standard explosion already follows one of them to the other plant.

I read CS_BOM_EXPL_MAT_V2 in an S/4HANA 2023 system. For each component with a special procurement key, form POS_PRUEFEN (include LCSS4F15) reads the key in T460A. If T460A-SOBES = 'P' (production in another plant), the BOM of that component is read in plant T460A-WRK02, so a multi-level explosion (MEHRS = 'X') already crosses the plant. The parameter SALWW = 'X' turns this off.

If SOBES = '7' (stock transfer), the explosion stays in the same plant. The component is procured there, not produced, so usually there is no BOM in that plant and the explosion stops. If your keys are type 7, this matches what you see in CS11, and then the custom logic makes sense.

What I would do differently:

  • Call CS_BOM_EXPL_MAT_V2 with MEHRS = 'X' and recurse only at the plant change, not level by level. STB already brings SOBSL on each line, so the lines to follow are the ones with SOBSL filled and SOBES = '7'.
  • Take the supplying plant from T460A-WRK02 (key WERKS + SOBSL), and pass the component quantity (STB-MNGLG) as EMENG, so the quantities from the next plant come already multiplied.
  • Keep a list of material + plant already on the current path. A stock transfer between two plants in both directions would loop forever.
  • Buffer the result per material + plant + alternative if the same subassembly repeats.

About DO...WHILE: ABAP has no DO...WHILE, but a WHILE loop over a work list (start with the top material, append each plant change you find) gives the same result as the recursion and is easier to debug. Either way, the loop guard is what matters.

I read the code, I didn't run a cross-plant explosion with real data. Do your keys have type 7 or P in T460A?

entry.content: @Sanan I owe you a correction first. In my first answer I wrote that point 1 is table USER_DEF_SETTING. I went back to the code today, and that table has no document type field at all. The default the app reads first is in table USER_PERS_DATA, field PURCHASINGDOCUMENTTYPE, read by employee (CL_MMPUR_REQ_ADMIN_DEF_HELPER, method GET_DOC_TYPE). If you checked USER_DEF_SETTING because of my answer, that one is on me. It matters for your test, because the BAdI is only asked when the other sources are empty. In CL_MMPUR_REQ_CONFIG_PROVIDER, method IF_MMPUR_REQ_CONFIG_PROVIDER~GET_DEFAULT_DOCUMENT_TYPE, the order is USER_PERS_DATA, then the org plan, then ESDUS, and only then the BAdI. So an NB in USER_PERS_DATA for your employee wins over the ZNB from your BAdI. Two more things in the same code could explain it. First, the type is set only once, when the cart (the draft header) is created: INITIALIZE_PURCHASEREQN_HDR fills it only if it is still empty, so a cart that existed before your BAdI keeps NB, and a new cart is the real test. Second, the BAdI receives CS_ITEM empty, because it is called once, in the constructor of CL_MMPUR_REQ_DEFLT_EXIT_HELPER. So a condition like IF cs_item-documenttype = 'NB' never matches, and the implementation needs to set cs_item-documenttype = 'ZNB' directly. If it still shows NB after that, an external breakpoint for the app user in that GET_DEFAULT_DOCUMENT_TYPE method shows which source answers. entry.title: Re: SAP RAP Question: Allowing Another User to Edit Drafts
entry.content:
Hi Ajay,

I was curious how Manage Purchase Orders does it, so I looked at it in an S/4HANA 2023 system. The surprise is that, in this release, the app doesn't use RAP draft at all. Its view C_PURCHASEORDERTP has draftEnabled: true with transactionalProcessingDelegated: true, which is the older BOPF-based draft, and the RAP BO R_PURCHASEORDERTP has no "with draft". So the app doesn't share drafts. It uses the takeover that an exclusive draft already has, and RAP has the same mechanism.

How it works:

  • The owner keeps the exclusive lock only for some time after the last change. The timings are in table SDRAFT_LC_CONFIG. The purchase order has no line of its own, so the <DEFAULT> line applies: event 02 (Relative Enqueue Expiry) is 900 seconds, so 15 minutes, and event 32 (Relative Draft Expiry) is 2,419,200 seconds, so 28 days, both counted from the last change. Several RAP BOs have their own lines in the same table, so RAP drafts follow the same rules.
  • Inside those 15 minutes, a second user who presses Edit is stopped by the lock.
  • After that, Fiori elements warns the second user about the unsaved changes of the first one. If they continue, the first user's draft is discarded and a new draft is created from the active data. In EML this is the Edit action with %param-preserve_changes = abap_false (the ABAP demo class CL_DEMO_RAP_MNGD_DRAFT_ACTNS uses this parameter).

So, for the "owner got ill or left" case, an exclusive draft already lets an authorized colleague continue, as long as Edit is allowed for them (authorization and feature control on Edit). The price is that the owner's unsaved changes are lost. If those changes must be kept, collaborative draft is the standard answer. I didn't find a standard way to hand over an exclusive draft together with its content.

I read the configuration and the code, I didn't test the takeover with two users. In your case, do the owner's changes need to survive, or is starting again from the active document acceptable?

entry.title: Re: Can we configure the maintenance order types in S/4 public cloud
entry.content: There is no way to “delete” or globally switch off a standard order type, but you can make it unavailable to users. Which method fits best depends on how strict you need to be. 1. Remove the order type from the Order Type configuration (cleanest approach) Maintenance order types are defined in: SPRO > Plant Maintenance and Customer Service > Maintenance and Service Processing > Maintenance and Service Orders > Functions and Settings for Order Types > Configure Order Types (OIOA) Order types are client-wide, so you cannot disable one for a single plant here. What you can do is stop it from being used by: Removing it from the Order Type-Dependent Parameters per Plant (Maintenance Plant-Dependent Parameters / Order type-dependent parameters, transaction OIOA / IMG node “Define Order Type-Dependent Parameters”). If an order type has no plant-specific parameters for a given plant, users cannot create orders of that type there. Not assigning it in the Print Control, Planner Group or Notification Type to Order Type settings (see point 3). 2. Authorization control (recommended for restricting users) Use the authorization object I_AUFART (Maintenance Order Type) and I_IWERK (Maintenance Planning Plant), in addition to I_BEGRP (Maintenance Planner Group): Object: I_AUFART Field AUFART: list only the order types users are allowed to use (e.g., PM01, PM02, PM03) Field ACTVT: 01 (create), 02 (change), 03 (display) If a user’s role does not include the overhead order type in I_AUFART with activity 01, they cannot create orders of that type. You can still allow display (03) so historical orders remain readable. Note: I_AUFART is checked as part of the PM order authorization (I_AUFART is checked together with I_ACTVT/ACTVT on order create/change) and also with the general order authorization I_AUFART/K_ORDER where applicable. Always confirm with SU53 / ST01 trace in your system. 3. Control which order types can be created from notifications In Notification Type > Order Type assignment (IMG: Maintenance and Service Notifications > Notification Creation > Notification Types > Define Notification Types, field “Order type”), the order type linked to a notification type is what gets proposed when users create an order from a notification. Make sure the irrelevant type is not assigned as default. 4. Screen/field control via Order Type configuration You can use Field Selection (OIOA / Order type settings) and Status Profile to prevent use, but this is not a true restriction. 5. Set a deletion flag / archive (for existing orders) If orders of this type already exist and you want the type retired, set the existing open orders to technical complete/closed or set a deletion flag, then handle the type via authorization as above.

entry.title: Enrichment of Solution Order Output with Information from Related Transactions Made Possible
entry.content:
Table of Contents

  • Table of Contents
  • Introduction

  • Getting Started
  • How to Set This Up for Solution Order Output?
  • Step 1: Define Your Fields
  • Step 2: Write the Calculation Logic
  • Step 3: Create a Custom Form
  • Step 3: See Your Fields in Action
  • Key Benefits
  • Benefit
  • What It Means
  • What You Can v/s Cannot Do
  • What Works Well
  • Points to Note
  • Best Practices
  • Conclusion

 

Introduction

When you create solution orders and generate output documents like order acknowledgements or invoices, you sometimes need to show information that is not stored in the database. Instead, you want to compute it based on other fields or data from related documents.

For example, you might want to display:

  • Pricing information from follow-on sales orders
  • Data from other business documents linked to the order
  • Information from custom business tables/CDS views
  • Special calculations based on order data

Consider an Example

Imagine a company that sells software solutions. When they create an order acknowledgement, they want to show:

  • The main order information (already in the system)
  • Special pricing discounts based on customer type (calculated field)
  • Expected delivery dates from linked sales orders (calculated field)
  • Processing agents’ contact information (calculated field)

Previously, the only solution was to create permanent custom fields in the database and store the calculated data there. But this wastes database space because you only need this information on the printed output.

Data Source extension and Calculated fields in that solve this problem.

Without this, customers would need to manually create custom database fields.

With data source extension and calculated fields, this information is computed only when printing the order acknowledgement. No database clutter, and your system stays focused on core business data.

 

Getting Started

What is a Data Source Extension?

A Data Source Extension lets you bring additional fields, either from existing data or calculated on the fly, into a user interface or output form, without changing the underlying database structure.

What are Calculated Fields?

They are temporary fields that the system computes on demand when generating an output form. The data is never stored in the database, so you save space and keep your system efficient.

To extend a data source of your solution order output forms, you need:

  • Access to the Custom Fields application in your system
  • Extensibility Expert and Configuration Expert - Business Process Configuration permissions
  • Basic knowledge of ABAP programming (for writing the calculation logic)
  • An existing solution order with output management already configured
  • Adobe LiveCycle Designer

The Process: You create a data source extension, define your fields, implement the calculation logic, define a custom for template, edit the form template to add calculated fields to the print form, upload the modified print form, assign the custom form template to the Solution Order application and test in print preview. Typically, this takes 3-4 hours.

 

How to Set This Up for Solution Order Output?

 Data Source Extensions work through three simple steps:

Step 1: Define Your Fields

Using the Custom Fields application, you create a "Data Source Extension" and define what calculated fields you need and publish. For each field, you specify:

  • Field name (what you'll call it)
  • Field type (text, number, date, currency, etc.)
  • Whether it's for the header or item level

Check: Data Source Extension is created successfully and status is "Published".

Check: The calculated fields are visible in the extension.

Step 2: Write the Calculation Logic

Next, once published you see the system creates a "BAdI Implementation" for your that calculates the field values. Implement the logic to assign a value to the calculated field you created in the previous step.

This program:

  • Receives the solution order data when a form is generated
  • Performs lookups or calculations using that data
  • Fills in the calculated field values
  • Returns the results to the form

Check: Custom Logic implementation has status "Published".

Check: No syntax errors in the BAdI Implementation.

Important: This program can only read data, not modify or save anything.

It's purely a calculation engine.

Step 3: Create a Custom Form

Create a custom form template using the Maintain Form Templates (F1434) application by copying the standard form template. Edit the standard form template using Adobe LiveCycle Designer.

The calculated fields appear in SrvcDocItemExtension entity for item fields and SrvcDocHeaderExtension for header fields in the data view.

Assign the custom form template to the output type BUSINESS_SOLUTION_ORDER

https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_S4HANA_ONPREMISE/8308e6d301d54584a33cd04a9861bc52/a5817657a11a0522e10000000a44147b.html?locale=en-US&state=TEST&version=2022.002

Step 3: See Your Fields in Action

When you generate a print preview or output form for a solution order, the system automatically calculates your custom fields and displays them on the form.

Hint: You can also use Manage Output Items (F2279)” Fiori application to trigger sending output for multiple Solution Orders at once. Additionally, if you want to schedule output for one or more than one Solution Orders based on certain conditions, you could do so using the “Schedule Output for Solution Orders (F9487)” Fiori application (available in 2608 or later).

 

 Key Benefits

 

Benefit

What It Means

Save Database Space

Data is calculated when needed, not stored permanently in the database

Flexible and Powerful

Pull data from other documents, tables, or perform complex calculations

No Database Quota Used

Calculated fields don't count against your system's extension field limits

Output Only

These fields appear only on printed forms i.e. they don't affect other apps or APIs

Easy to Maintain

Changing calculation logic doesn't require database migrations

 

What You Can v/s Cannot Do

What Works Well

  • Display text, numbers, dates, and currency amounts
  • Include information from related documents or tables
  • Perform calculations and lookups
  • Use in print preview and output forms
  • Show data from custom business tables

Points to Note

Read-Only: The calculation program will not modify, create, or save any business data.

Output Only: These fields appear only on printed forms. They don't show up in other apps, reports, or APIs.

No Filtering or Searching: You cannot search or filter orders by calculated field values.

Limited Field Types: Only text and numeric field types are supported. Currency amounts support up to 2 decimal places.

Not for Analytics: Calculated fields cannot be used in analytical queries or reporting views.

 

Best Practices

Performance First: Always design your calculations to work efficiently with large batches of data. The system sends all records to your calculation program at once.

Focus on Display: Use calculated fields only for information that needs to appear on forms. Don't try to use them for filtering, searching, or reporting.

Keep Logic Simple: Complex calculations might slow down form generation. Test your calculations with real data volumes.

Document Your Fields: Clearly name and describe your calculated fields so other team members understand what they contain.

 

Conclusion

Make use of data source extension feature to enhance your solution order output forms without compromising system efficiency. By computing information on-demand, you get flexible, rich documents while keeping your database clean and optimized. Whether you need to display related order information, custom calculations, or data from external sources, calculated fields provide a modern and maintainable solution.

System Information: Available in SAP S/4HANA Cloud 2608 and later.

Related Features: Output Management, Form Data Provider, Data Source Extensions, Custom Fields, Custom Logic, Solution Order.

entry.title: SAP S/4HANA Outbound IDoc Integration With SAP CPI: Complete Configuration Guide
entry.content:
Introduction

Many integration scenarios require SAP S/4HANA to send master or transactional data to external systems. IDocs are a standard way to do this, and SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) can receive them over HTTPS. Setting this up involves several connected pieces: a logical system, an RFC destination, an XML HTTP port, a partner profile, and a distribution model. Missing any one of them causes errors that can be hard to trace.

In this blog, I walk through the complete outbound IDoc configuration from SAP S/4HANA 2023 to SAP Cloud Integration, using MATMAS as the example. You will see how to configure each component, test the connection, trigger an IDoc, and monitor it on both the SAP and CPI sides. This blog is useful for SAP integration consultants and developers who are new to IDoc-to-CPI connectivity.

Complete Guide to SAP S/4HANA Outbound IDoc Configuration with SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI)


Prerequisites

  • SAP S/4HANA 2023
  • SAP Integration Suite
  • SAP GUI
  • Authorization for ALE configuration
  • Deployed CPI iFlow
  • Service Key
  • SSL Certificates

 End-to-End Integration Flow: SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end communication flow of an outbound IDoc from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration, highlighting the key SAP components involved in secure IDoc transmission.

Configuration Steps

 


Configure the Logical System :
Step : 1
       You can create a logical system either by using transaction SALE or directly through BD54. If you use SALE, navigate to Basic Settings → Logical Systems → Define Logical System. This opens the same configuration screen as transaction BD54.


In the Define Logical System screen, click New Entries, create a logical system by providing a unique Logical System Name and a meaningful Description, and then save the configuration.


The logical system uniquely identifies the sender (SAP S/4HANA) and the receiver (SAP Cloud Integration) during ALE/IDoc communication and is required for successful outbound IDoc processing.

Create the Integration Flow in SAP Cloud Integration
Before configuring the RFC destination in SAP S/4HANA, create and deploy an Integration Flow (iFlow) in SAP Cloud Integration.

Configure the Sender Adapter as an IDoc Adapter and maintain the required sender endpoint address. After deploying the iFlow, navigate to Monitor → Manage Integration Content, select the deployed integration flow, and copy the generated HTTPS endpoint URL. This endpoint will be used while configuring the RFC destination in SAP S/4HANA.

    Note: For security reasons, the tenant host name shown in the screenshots has been blurred.



Importing the SAP Cloud Integration SSL Certificate into SAP S/4HANA (STRUST)Before SAP S/4HANA can securely communicate with SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) over HTTPS, the SSL certificates of your SAP Integration Suite tenant must be imported into the SAP Trust Manager (STRUST). This establishes a trusted SSL connection and prevents certificate validation errors during IDoc transmission.

Step 1: Export the SAP Integration Suite Certificates

  1. Open your deployed SAP Cloud Integration iFlow URL in your web browser.
  2. Click the View Site Information (🔒 Lock icon) beside the URL.
  3. Select Connection is secure.
  4. Click Certificate is valid.
  5. Open the Details tab.
  6. Under Certificate Hierarchy, export the following three certificates individually:
  • DigiCert TLS RSA4096 Root G5
  • DigiCert G5 TLS RSA4096 SHA384 2021 CA1
  • *.it-cpitrial03.cfapps.ap21.hana.ondemand.com (Your SAP Integration Suite tenant certificate)

Note: Save all three certificates in a local folder. These certificates establish the complete trust chain required for secure HTTPS communication.
Step 2: Copy the Certificates to the SAP Server

Copy the exported certificate files to the SAP application server (or a location accessible from SAP GUI). This allows SAP to import the certificates into its Trust Manager.


Step 3: Import the Certificates in STRUST

  1. Execute transaction STRUST.
  2. Expand SSL Client (Anonymous) (or the SSL Client PSE used by your RFC destination).
  3. Click Import Certificate.
  4. Browse to the folder where the certificates are stored.
  5. Select one certificate and click Continue.
  6. If prompted with the SAP GUI Security dialog, click Allow to grant access to the selected file.
  7. Repeat the same process for all three certificates.
  8. After importing all certificates, click Add to Certificate List and Save the changes.

Important: Import the certificates in the same order as shown in the certificate hierarchy (Root CA → Intermediate CA → SAP Integration Suite Tenant Certificate). This ensures the complete certificate chain is trusted by SAP.

Why is STRUST Configuration Required?
STRUST is used to establish trust between SAP S/4HANA and external HTTPS systems. Since SAP Cloud Integration communicates over SSL/TLS, SAP S/4HANA must trust the server certificate presented by the SAP Integration Suite tenant. Without importing these certificates, the RFC destination may fail with SSL handshake or certificate validation errors.

Once the certificates are successfully imported, SAP S/4HANA can securely send outbound IDocs to SAP Cloud Integration through the configured XML HTTP Port and RFC destination.

Create the RFC Destination
What is an RFC Destination?

An RFC (Remote Function Call) an RFC Destination defines the communication settings that allow SAP S/4HANA to connect to external systems. In this scenario, it enables SAP S/4HANA to securely send outbound IDocs to SAP Cloud Integration over HTTPS.

You can create the RFC destination either by navigating through the SALE transaction or directly using SM59.
If you use SALE, navigate to:

Basic Settings → Communication → Create RFC Connections

This option opens the same configuration screen as transaction SM59, where you can create the HTTP RFC destination.

The Configuration of RFC Connections screen displays various types of RFC destinations that can be used to communicate with different systems. For communication between SAP S/4HANA and SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI), select HTTP Connections to External Server, as SAP CPI is accessed through an HTTPS endpoint.

To create a new RFC destination, select HTTP Connections to External Server and click Create, as shown in the figure below.

In the Create Destination dialog, enter a meaningful destination name (for example, RFC_JD_CPI) and select G – HTTP Connection to External Server as the Connection Type. The appearance of this dialog may vary slightly depending on your SAP S/4HANA release, but the required Connection Type (G) remains the same.

After choosing the destination name and connection type, click the Continue (✔) button to create the RFC destination. In the next step, configure the Technical Settings, Logon & Security, and SSL parameters using the SAP CPI endpoint and SAP BTP credentials obtained from the deployed integration flow.

  Note: The screenshots in this blog are based on SAP S/4HANA 2023. Depending on your SAP release, the screen layout may differ slightly; however, the configuration steps and required settings remain the same.

Configure the RFC Destination
After creating the RFC destination, maintain the required connection details in the Technical Settings and Logon & Security tabs.

Technical Settings

Open the Technical Settings tab and maintain the following information:

  • Description – Provide a meaningful description for the RFC destination (for example, Secure communication from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration).
  • Host – Enter the SAP Cloud Integration tenant host name copied from the deployed iFlow endpoint.
  • Port – Specify 443 for secure HTTPS communication.
  • Path Prefix – Enter only the endpoint path generated by the deployed iFlow (for example, /cxf/JD/klaus/out).

Note: The endpoint URL displayed in Monitor → Manage Integration Content consists of the Host and Path Prefix. In the RFC destination, enter the Host and Path Prefix in their respective fields instead of pasting the complete URL.

Logon & Security

Next, navigate to the Logon & Security tab.

Under Logon Procedure, select Basic Authentication and maintain the authentication credentials for SAP Cloud Integration. It is highly recommended to use the Client ID and Client Secret obtained from the SAP Integration Suite Standard Service Key, as this is the recommended authentication method for production environments. Alternatively, for development or testing purposes, you can authenticate using your SAP Cloud Integration tenant user ID and password. If you are unsure how to obtain these credentials, refer to the SAP documentation using the link provided below.


After entering the credentials, scroll down to the Security Options section.

Enable SSL by changing the status from Inactive to Active. For the SSL Client PSE, select either:

  • DEFAULT SSL Client (Standard) (recommended), or
  • Anonymous SSL Client, depending on your organization's security requirements.

This configuration enables secure HTTPS communication between SAP S/4HANA and SAP Cloud Integration.

Test the Connection

After saving the RFC destination, execute the Connection Test to verify that SAP S/4HANA can reach the SAP Cloud Integration endpoint.

When testing an IDoc Sender Adapter, receiving an HTTP Response Status 500 (Internal Server Error) is generally expected. The IDoc sender endpoint is designed to process IDoc requests and does not respond to a simple HTTP GET request issued by the connection test.

The important point is that the connection successfully reaches the SAP Cloud Integration tenant, confirming that:

  • The Host, Port, and Path Prefix are configured correctly.
  • SSL communication is established successfully.
  • SAP S/4HANA can communicate with the SAP Cloud Integration tenant.



    Examples:
  • HTTP 401 – Invalid authentication credentials.
  • HTTP 403 – Authorization issue.
  • HTTP 500 – Connection established; check the CPI iFlow and endpoint.
  • SSLHandshakeException – Certificate not imported in STRUST.

No communication IDoc generated – Verify Partner Profile, Distribution Model, Logical System, and Message Type.

Create an XML HTTP Port (WE21)

The next step is to create an XML HTTP Port, which is used to route outbound IDocs from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) through the configured RFC destination.

Navigate to transaction WE21. In the Ports tree, expand XML HTTP and click the Create icon (or press F7) to create a new XML HTTP port.

Enter a meaningful Port name (for example, PORT_JD_CI) and maintain an appropriate Description. In the RFC Destination field, enter the RFC destination created in the previous step (for example, RFC_JD_CPI).

For the remaining settings:

  • Set the Content Type to application/x-sap.idoc.
  • Select the SOAP Protocol checkbox.
  • Leave the remaining settings with their default values unless your project requires additional configuration.

After maintaining all the required fields, save the XML HTTP port.

This XML HTTP port is now linked to the RFC destination and will be assigned to the outbound partner profile in WE20. During IDoc processing, SAP uses this port to transmit outbound IDocs securely to the SAP Cloud Integration endpoint.


Create the Partner Profile (WE20)

A partner profile defines how IDocs are exchanged between the sender and receiver systems. It contains the communication settings required for outbound and inbound IDoc processing, such as the partner, message type, port, and IDoc type.

Navigate to transaction WE20 to create the partner profile. Under Partner Type, select LS (Logical System) and create a new partner profile.



Maintain the following details:

  • Partner No. – Enter the Logical System name created earlier in BD54 (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).
  • Partner Type – Select LS (Logical System).

Next, under the Post Processing: Valid Processors tab, maintain the following:

Type – Select the appropriate processor type based on your requirement. In this example, US (User) is selected.
Agent – Enter the corresponding processor value. In this example, the SAP user ID is maintained as the Agent.
Language – Set the language to EN (English).
After maintaining these details, save the partner profile. In the next step, configure the Outbound Parameters by assigning the required Message Type, Receiver Port, and Basic Type for outbound IDoc communication.

Configure Outbound Parameters (WE20)

After saving the partner profile, the next step is to configure the Outbound Parameters. In the Outbound section, click the Add icon (highlighted in the screenshot) to create a new outbound parameter for the partner profile.



Maintain the following details:

  • Message Type – Enter the required message type (for example, MATMAS).
  • Receiver Port – Select the XML HTTP port created earlier in WE21 (for example, PORT_JD_CI).
  • Output Mode – Select Pass IDoc Immediately to transmit the IDoc as soon as it is generated.
  • Basic Type – Select the IDoc basic type that corresponds to your integration scenario (for example, MATMAS07).

After maintaining the required fields, save the outbound parameter configuration.

Message Type identifies the business message being exchanged between systems, such as MATMAS for Material Master or DEBMAS for Customer Master.

Basic Type defines the IDoc structure, including its segments and fields, that is used to exchange the selected business message.

Configure the Distribution Model (BD64)

The final ALE configuration step is to maintain the Distribution Model, which defines the sender, receiver, and message types that are allowed for IDoc distribution.

Navigate to transaction BD64, or use the following path in SALE:

SALE - Modeling and Implementing Business Processes → Maintain Distribution Model and Distribute Views




Open the Distribution Model and click the Change (Edit) icon. Next, choose Create Model View and enter a meaningful Short Text and Technical Name for your integration scenario (for example, JD_CPI_Idoc_Models). Save the model view.

After creating the model view, select it and click Add Message Type.

Maintain the following details:

  • Sender – Select the logical system of your SAP S/4HANA system.
  • Receiver – Select the receiver logical system created earlier in BD54 and used in WE20 (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).
  • Message Type – Select the same message type configured in the partner profile (for example, MATMAS).


    Save the configuration.

Note: A single distribution model can contain multiple message types. If your integration scenario requires sending different business objects (such as MATMAS, DEBMAS, CREMAS, or ORDERS), you can add multiple message types under the same model view. This enables SAP S/4HANA to route different outbound IDocs to the same receiver logical system.

Test the Outbound IDoc (WE19)

What is WE19?

WE19 is the SAP IDoc Test Tool, used to create, simulate, and trigger IDocs without executing an actual business transaction. It is commonly used to validate IDoc configurations and verify end-to-end communication between SAP S/4HANA and external systems such as SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI).

Use Case: WE19 is primarily used by developers and integration consultants to test IDoc interfaces, validate partner profile configurations, and troubleshoot integration issues before moving them to production.

Trigger the IDoc

Navigate to transaction WE19 and select Basic Type. Enter the required Message Type (for example, MATMAS) and click Execute.

In the IDoc structure, select the EDI_DC40 (EDIDC) control record and maintain the following details:

  • Receiver Port – XML HTTP Port created in WE21 (for example, PORT_JD_CI).
  • Receiver Partner No. – Logical System created for SAP CPI (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).
  • Receiver Partner Type – LS (Logical System).
  • Sender Port – SAP sender port.
  • Sender Partner No. – Sender logical system of SAP S/4HANA.
  • Sender Partner Type – LS (Logical System).
  • Message Type – MATMAS.


After maintaining the control record, save the changes and choose Standard Outbound Processing.

An Outbound Processing of IDoc dialog appears. Confirm the processing by clicking Continue. You will then receive the confirmation message "IDoc sent by HTTP in XML format". After successful processing, SAP displays the generated IDoc Number, confirming that the IDoc has been created and stored in the database.

Verify the Message in SAP Cloud Integration

Once the IDoc is triggered, navigate to Monitor → Message Processing in SAP Cloud Integration. You can verify that the IDoc has been received successfully.

As shown in the payload, the control record (EDI_DC40) contains the sender and receiver information configured earlier, including the Sender Logical System, Receiver Logical System, Receiver Port, Partner Type, and Message Type. This confirms that the configurations maintained in BD54, WE21, WE20, and BD64 have been applied successfully during IDoc processing.


Alternative Method to Trigger IDocs

In addition to WE19, IDocs can also be generated directly from business transactions.

  • BD10 – Trigger Material Master (MATMAS) IDocs.
  • BD12 – Trigger Customer Master (DEBMAS) IDocs.

These transactions generate IDocs from actual master data records instead of creating a test IDoc. Simply select the required material or customer record, specify the appropriate Message Type, and execute the transaction. SAP automatically creates and sends the IDoc using the configured Partner Profile, Port, and Distribution Model.

Note: WE19 is ideal for interface testing and troubleshooting, whereas BD10 and BD12 are typically used to send actual business master data to the target system.

Trigger Material Master IDoc Using BD10

BD10 is used to generate and send Material Master (MATMAS) IDocs from SAP S/4HANA to external systems. Unlike WE19, which is mainly used for testing, BD10 sends IDocs based on actual material master data maintained in SAP.

Execute transaction BD10 and enter the following details:

  • Material – Enter a valid Material Number.
  • Message Type – Enter MATMAS.
  • Logical System – Enter the receiver logical system created in BD54 (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).

Note: Ensure that the material number is valid and maintained in SAP. If the material does not exist or the logical system/message type is configured incorrectly, the IDoc will not be generated.


Click Execute. A confirmation popup appears stating "1 master IDoc set up for message type MATMAS." Click Continue



A second confirmation popup displays "1 communication IDoc(s) generated for message type MATMAS." Click Continue again. SAP then generates the IDoc and sends it to SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) using the configured Partner Profile, XML HTTP Port, and Distribution Model.



If the popup displays 0 communication IDoc(s), no IDoc has been generated. In this case, verify that the Material Number, Message Type, and Logical System are configured correctly.

Similarly, to trigger Customer Master IDocs, use transaction BD12, enter the required customer details, Message Type, and Logical System, and execute the transaction. The process is the same as BD10.

Monitor IDoc Status (WE02)

After triggering the IDoc using WE19, BD10, or BD12, you can monitor its processing status using transaction WE02 (IDoc Display). This transaction provides detailed information about generated IDocs, including the IDoc number, Message Type, Basic Type, Partner, Port, Direction, Processing Status, and error details.

In the screenshot below, multiple outbound MATMAS IDocs are displayed with different processing statuses.


Common Outbound IDoc Status Codes

Status

Description

30

IDoc ready for dispatch. The IDoc has been created successfully and is waiting to be sent to the configured port.

03

Data passed to port successfully. The IDoc was successfully sent to the configured XML HTTP Port and forwarded to SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI). This indicates successful outbound processing.

02

Error passing data to port. The IDoc could not be sent due to a communication or configuration issue, such as an incorrect RFC Destination, SSL configuration, authentication, or network problem. Open the IDoc to view the detailed error message.

29

Error in ALE service. An error occurred during ALE processing before the IDoc could be sent. Verify the Partner Profile, Distribution Model, Logical System, and Port configuration.

32

IDoc was passed to the application successfully. This status is mainly seen for inbound processing, indicating that the receiving application processed the IDoc successfully.

51

Application document not posted. The IDoc reached the receiving application, but processing failed due to business or application errors. This status is commonly seen for inbound IDocs.

53

Application document posted successfully. The IDoc was processed successfully, and the business document was created. This status is commonly seen for inbound IDocs.

Note: For outbound IDocs sent from SAP S/4HANA to SAP CPI, the most commonly encountered status codes are 30, 03, and 02.

Conclusion

In this blog, we configured an end-to-end outbound IDoc integration from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration using MATMAS as the example. We created the RFC Destination, XML HTTP Port, Partner Profile and Distribution Model, and then triggered and monitored the IDoc using WE19 and BD10. The same approach can be extended to other message types such as DEBMAS, CREMAS, ORDERS and INVOIC with minimal configuration changes.

I hope this guide helps you set up your own outbound IDoc scenarios. If you have questions or run into issues, please leave a comment below. I’d also encourage you to follow the SAP Integration Suite and SAP S/4HANA tags for related content.

entry.title: Step Zero Before You Put AI on an SAP S/4HANA Process
entry.content:
The person who always closes the purchasing process goes on vacation. Their replacement has the manual, the user ID and access to S/4HANA. By mid-morning, they have already asked five times how to move forward. None of the answers were in the manual.

Now swap the replacement for a Joule agent or an automated workflow. It won’t ask five times. It will do exactly what the documentation says.

 

 

 

That is the question worth asking before you put AI or automation on a process in SAP S/4HANA: is the process written down, or is it held up by the people who know how to run it?

Today there are three good guides for governing AI in business processes: COSO’s guidance on generative AI, FEI’s framework on internal control over financial reporting, and SAP’s playbook for ERP automation. All three agree on the fundamentals: AI in a process needs controls, and those controls must be testable. SAP’s playbook even asks teams to map decision points and codify business rules. What none of them offers is a way to check whether the process is actually written down, or held up by people.

If it isn’t, something happens that nobody sees: the automation passes its tests, because the tests have the same gap as the documentation.

These four tests help you find out first. Each one runs on what is already in S/4HANA, with no new tools and no budget.

1. The replacement test

Give the process documentation to someone who doesn’t run the process, and ask them to run it end to end in the test system, using only what is written.

Threshold: if they need to ask more than three times, the process is not described. It is held up by a person.

It is the most uncomfortable test and the fastest: half a day. And it leaves no room for interpretation: either the purchase order reaches the invoice with what is written, or it doesn’t.

2. The exception test

Take one month of purchase orders and journal entries, and count how many were resolved outside the normal path. S/4HANA keeps a trail:

  • Purchase orders changed after release: every change is stored in change documents (tables CDHDR and CDPOS, object class EINKBELEG).
  • Purchase orders without a prior requisition or outside a contract, when the procedure says otherwise: on the PO item, the requisition field (EKPO-BANFN) and the contract field (EKPO-KONNR) are empty.
  • Manual journal entries at month-end: filter them by document type (SA in the standard) and separate them from the ones the system posts on its own.

Threshold: if more than one in ten needed a decision that is not in the procedure, the process runs on unwritten judgment.

One clarification: recurring manual entries that are on the closing checklist don’t count. The ones that count are those nobody could explain with the procedure in hand.

Every “it depends” is a rule that exists and was never written down. “If the supplier is new, I ask for approval even when the amount doesn’t require it.” An agent doesn’t know that rule.

Time: one day.

3. The repeated-question test

For one week, log every question to the help desk or to key users about this process, and the transaction or Fiori app where it came up.

Threshold: if the same question shows up twice, the documentation describes something different from what is actually done.

This test doesn’t measure people. It measures the distance between the document and the operation.

Time: one week, alongside normal work.

4. The control test

List the controls in the process and ask, for each one, where it lives:

  • Configured in S/4HANA (automated control): a release strategy or approval workflow, a required field, data the system won’t let you save if it’s missing.
  • Or in a person (manual control): someone who reviews a report and “notices.”

Threshold: if the control depends on someone looking at a report, it won’t survive automation.

Configured controls scale on their own, as long as nobody turns them off or works around them. Controls that depend on a person noticing something odd stop existing when volume goes up and nobody is looking.

Time: one day with the process owner.

What to do with the result

None of the four is a pass or fail for the whole process. What they give you is a map: which part of the process is defined, and which part is held up by people who know.

The defined part is ready to automate in S/4HANA. The rest has to be written down first, and the team bringing the tool can’t do that work. It’s done by the people who know the process.

The thresholds are a starting point, not a standard. Adjust them to the risk: a financial close deserves a stricter bar than an office supplies purchase.

Why it matters more than it seems

FEI’s framework lists performance testing among its control approaches: comparing what the AI produces against what is considered correct. It is the most rigorous approach. And “correct” is built from how the process runs today.

If part of that “how” was never written down, the reference is incomplete from day one. The automation passes the test, because the test has the same gap as the documentation. Nothing fails, no alert goes off, and the lost judgment doesn’t show up on any S/4HANA dashboard.

What this does not mean

It doesn’t mean documenting everything before automating anything. That would be the perfect excuse to never start.

It means the process description stops being one more project deliverable and becomes part of the control system. It changes category and it changes owner: it no longer belongs to the project team. It belongs to the process owner.

 

If you have run any of these tests on a real process in S/4HANA, tell me which one your process failed. In my experience, the second one surprises people the most.

References

  • COSO, Achieving Effective Internal Control Over Generative AI (February 2026).
  • FEI, Committee on Corporate Reporting, AI Framework: Internal Control Over Financial Reporting (June 2026).
  • SAP, ERP Automation at Scale: A Playbook for AI-Enabled Operations (SAP blog).

entry.title: Error Message "Buyer ID is mandatory if Buyer VAT Registration Number is not provided"
entry.content:
SAP DRC / ZATCA E-Invoicing: Resolving the Error “Buyer ID Is Mandatory if Buyer VAT Registration Number Is Not Provided”

Introduction

While submitting invoices to the ZATCA (Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority) portal in Saudi Arabia, you may encounter the following error:

“Buyer ID is mandatory if Buyer VAT Registration Number is not provided.”

This error can occur when the buyer's tax information is not maintained in accordance with the requirements of the ZATCA e-invoicing integration in SAP.

In this blog, I’ll explain a potential resolution for this issue, particularly when processing invoices for local and foreign customers.

Understanding the Issue

In the 2023 version of the applicable SAP/ZATCA setup, the accepted buyer tax code for local customers was required to be maintained as SA0 in the relevant Tax Code segment of the Customer Business Partner.

Even when the customer's VAT/TIN number and other tax details were maintained according to business requirements, invoices could encounter validation issues if the required tax code was not assigned correctly.

A similar issue may arise when processing invoices for foreign customers, where maintaining the local customer tax code may not satisfy the applicable validation requirements.

Solution: Maintain the Appropriate Buyer Tax Code

Based on the SAP KBA recommendation referenced for this scenario, the buyer tax code should be maintained according to whether the customer is local or foreign.

Customer category Buyer Tax Code

Local customerSA0
Foreign customerSA1

Step 1: Identify the Customer Category

Determine whether the customer associated with the invoice is a local Saudi customer or a foreign customer.

Step 2: Check the Customer Business Partner

Open the relevant Customer Business Partner in SAP and navigate to the applicable tax-related section.

Verify the buyer tax code maintained in the Tax Code segment.

Step 3: Maintain the Appropriate Tax Code

  • For local customers: Maintain tax code SA0.

  • For foreign customers: Maintain tax code SA1, as recommended in the relevant SAP KBA for this scenario.

Ensure that the customer's other tax-related information, including the VAT/TIN number where applicable, is maintained according to business requirements.

Here, in the above image, the Customer belongs to UAE Region. And since this is a case of Foreign Customer, Tax Code: SA1 is maintained.

Step 4: Resubmit the Invoice

After correcting the customer master data, retry the invoice submission to the ZATCA portal and verify whether the validation error has been resolved.

Key Takeaway

When troubleshooting the ZATCA validation error “Buyer ID is mandatory if Buyer VAT Registration Number is not provided,” check the buyer tax code maintained in the Customer Business Partner, especially for foreign customers.

For the specific configuration described in this scenario:

  • Local customers → SA0

  • Foreign customers → SA1

Correctly maintaining the buyer tax code can help address validation issues during invoice submission.

Note: The applicable tax-code requirements may depend on the SAP solution, configuration, and version of the ZATCA integration. Validate the recommendation against the relevant SAP KBA and your system's implementation before applying it in production.

Conclusion

Accurate customer master data is essential for successful SAP-to-ZATCA e-invoicing integration. Checking the buyer tax code for local and foreign customers is a useful troubleshooting step when investigating buyer identification validation errors.

I hope this helps other SAP professionals working on Saudi Arabia e-invoicing implementations and support issues.

entry.title: Introducing On-Premise Extractor, Advance Scalability & Security

Running data integrations from your on-premises systems shouldn't mean choosing between reliability, security, and scale. For enterprises powering mission-critical process intelligence, the connection between your systems and the cloud has to simply work — every hour of every day. 

The previous On-Premises Extractor served customers well, but enterprise expectations have moved on. 

  • A single extractor instance meant a single point of failure — and possible disconnections. 
  • Security standards had advanced beyond shared-secret authentication. 
  • The underlying Java runtime was aging, creating a growing compliance concern. 

What's new 
The new On-Premises Extractor delivers four things that matter most to enterprise teams: 

  • High availability, built in. Run multiple extractor instances under a single configuration. If one instance goes down for maintenance or hits a network issue, the others keep serving extractions — no single point of failure, no interruption to your pipelines. 
  • Modern, password-less security. Key-pair authentication replaces legacy shared-secret credentials. Your private key never leaves your environment; only the public key is registered in the cloud. 
  • Enterprise-grade scalability. Add instances to grow with your workloads — no architecture changes required. Distribute load across devices and networks for resilience. 
  • A current, compliant foundation. Built on Java 25, with a redesigned setup experience and stable, persistent communication over Long polling.

Possible disconnections, single instance 

High availability, horizontal scaling (multiple instances) 

Basic authentication 

Secure Key-Pair authentication 

Java 17 (aging) 

Modern Java 25 

Websocket communication 

Persistent communication with HTTPS Long Polling

If you're currently using the On-Premises Extractor, migration to the new version is required before the current version reaches end of maintenance.

  • Step 7: Run the new on-prem extractor via ./start.sh

entry.title: CDS Table Entities - Definition of Fields: built-in types and type mappings
entry.content:
The next two parts of the series will dive deeper into field definitions in CDS table entities; this article starting out with ABAP built-in types, and the next focusing on data elements and CDS types. In case you missed the previous post, "Getting Started with CDS Table Entities", you can read it here.

How to define fields in CDS table entities

Table entities are composed of a list of field definitions, all of which follow the structure:

field_definition ::=
    [field_annotation]
    [key] field_name : type_reference [null];

An example field list could look like this:

@ClientHandling.type: #CLIENT_DEPENDENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass: #APPLICATION_DATA
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Mountains of the world'
define table entity ZAK_MOUNTAINS
{
  key mountain_id    : abap.raw(16);
      mountain_name  : abap.char(80);
      mountain_range : abap.char(30);
      description    : abap.string null; 
      @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'height_unit'
      height      : abap.quan(7,2);
      height_unit : abap.unit;      
      first_ascent   : abap.datn; // date of first ascent
      first_ascent_at : abap.utclong; // timestamp of first ascent
      num_routes   : abap.int4;   // known routes to the summit  
      @Semantics.spatialData.srid.value: '0'
      location : abap.geom_ewkb null; 
}

As you can see above, the syntax is still very similar to how fields are defined in classic dictionary tables. Primary key fields are defined with the keyword key, just like one would expect it in classic tables as well.

Fields that contain the keyword null are nullable, meaning these columns may contain SQL null values. Unlike classic tables, CDS table entities officially support nullability. The reason for this is that some datatypes do not have a suitable default value on the database, so they require the null keyword when used in the field definition (a more detailed post on this topic will follow later).

While classic tables contain an explicit client field with type mandt in their field list, CDS table entities handle client dependency implicitly, similarly to CDS view entities. This means that it is no longer necessary to define an explicit client field in the field list. Instead, client dependency is handled via header annotation @ClientHandling.type (more on this will follow in a dedicated article as well). This change in behavior was motivated by two factors: First, aligning the client handling behavior with CDS view entities rather than classic tables leads to more consistency in terms of behavior across different CDS objects. And secondly, since the client field does not contain any true business payload but rather a system-managed key for tenant isolation, it is not necessary to declare it explicitly in the data model.

Numeric types

Let’s start with the easiest kind of datatype: the numeric types. The following numeric built-in types are supported in CDS table entities:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

abap.int1

b (1-byte int)

TINYINT

abap.int2

INT2

s (2-byte int)

SMALLINT

abap.int4

INT4

i (4-byte int)

INTEGER

abap.int8

INT8

int8

BIGINT

abap.dec

DEC

p (packed)

DECIMAL

abap.decfloat16

DECFLOAT16

decfloat16

SMALLDECIMAL

abap.decfloat34

DECFLOAT34

decfloat34

DECIMAL

abap.fltp

FLTP

f (float)

DOUBLE

It should be noted that in classic tables, abap.int1 is mapped to SMALLINT, whereas CDS table entities map this type tp TINYINT. Not only does this save space (which is precious!), it also results in congruent domains in ABAP and the database. This datatype is the only case so far where the type mapping differs between classic tables and CDS table entities.

While abap.dec and abap.decfloat34 are both mapped to DECIMAL on HANA, these two are fundamentally different types with different behavior. The type abap.dec requires two arguments, declaring an explicit length and decimal places via precision (p) and scale (s). The resulting HANA type is therefore a fixed-point DECIMAL(p,s) with hard maximum of p total digits and exactly s fractional digits.
On the other hand, abap.decfloat34 does not have any arguments. It maps to a decimal floating-point number where the precision and scale of the stored value are determined by the value itself. This difference has some practical implications, for example when performing a CAST operation between dec and decfloat34 in CDS.
Similarly, the smaller datatype abap.decfloat16, which is mapped to SMALLDECIMAL, also represents a floating-point decimal. However, unlike abap.decfloat34 which has a capacity of 16 bytes with up to 34 decimal digits, abap.decfloat16 only has a capacity for 8 bytes with up to 16 decimal digits in its coefficient.
Lastly, columns typed as abap.fltp store binary floating-point numbers, meaning only integer powers of 2 can be represented exactly. This can lead to ambiguities and  rounding errors (e.g., after divisions by powers of 10), which is also the reason abap.fltp cannot be used as datatype for key fields in CDS.

Since developing new objects always comes with getting rid of some old pain points from the past, we chose to deprecate some types as well:

abap.df34_dec

While types DF16_DEC and DF34_DEC (decimal floating point stored in binary coded decimal format) can be changed to type DEC without adjustments on the database, DF16_RAW and DF34_RAW (stored in binary format) require a table conversion to be changed to DEC or DECFLOAT16 or DECFLOAT34, respectively. DF16_SCL and DF34_SCL (stored in binary format with specific scaling) as well as PREC are officially obsolete. Since HANA has native built-in decfloat support, the old decfloat types listed above are no longer needed and therefore deprecated.

Character-like types

The following character-like types are supported as well:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.char

CHAR

c

NVARCHAR

abap.string

STRG

string

NCLOB

abap.sstring

SSTR

abap.numc

n

NVARCHAR

abap.lang

LANG

c

NVARCHAR

In CDS table entites, abap.string will no longer have a length component besides abap.string(0) (a length of zero means „unlimited length“). This means we always consider strings to have no length limits. An important distinction however is that "no length limit" does not mean "infinite storage". It simply means that the type itself does not impose a limit to how long a string value can be. The underlying NCLOB column in the database still has a physical ceiling which belongs to the infrastructure layer.
Due to the lack of suitable default values for NCLOBS on the database, abap.string is also denoted as a nullable type, i.e., it is one of the datatypes which require the null keyword (along with abap.rawstring, see below). Not adding this keyword will result in syntax errors.
Unlike abap.string, abap.sstring can also be used in where clauses, join conditions and indices.

Can‘t we just use NUMC for every number? – Our recommendations

The datatype abap.numc is one of the most frequently used types, e.g. to denote different kinds of IDs such as buyer IDs or item numbers. It is a character-like type that accepts only digits, and maps to NVARCHAR on the database just like any other CHAR-like type. Since abap.numc is digit-only and auto-pads with leading zeros, it appears more controlled at handling numbers than a plain CHARat first glance. However, it lacks all of the actual semantics of numeric types (such as arithmetic, ordering, or range checks). Overusing abap.numc can therefore lead to potential problems:

  • Since NUMC is a character-like type on the database, SQL aggregations such as AVG, SUM or MAX cannot be used on NUMC-fields. Moreover, there isn’t any digit-only enforcement on the database either: In the old dynpro world, screen field validation would at least catch non-digit input at the UI layer, however, In a RAP/Fiori Elements world, that enforcement is gone unless you explicitly add a validation in the behavior definition.
  • Comparisons with other CHAR-fields may lead to unexpected results due to implicit conversion rules if the CHAR-field is not purely numeric (e. g., in where-clauses).
  • NUMC-fields of different lengths are not cast-compatible (e. g. abap.numc(5) and abap.numc(6)), resulting in errors when attempting to join similar looking „numbers“ across different entities.
  • NUMC is only compatible with CHAR and other NUMC fields of equal or greater length in comparisons and ON-conditions. For example, defining a NUMC key in a child entity and attempting to join it to a parent which contains a NUMC-field of a different length will result in an activation error. It can only be fixed by realigning lengths, which may even require a table migration if the table already contains data.
  • Using NUMC in Native SQL and AMDP is explicitly discouraged in the docs, as conversions in the Native SQL interface should be avoided whenever possible.
  • NUMC fields in OData services typically need explicit handling to avoid the leading zeros being stripped, or the field being mistyped on the consumer side.

There is a legitimate use case for abap.numc though, which is whenever there are fixed-length numeric identifiers where leading zeros are part of the business meaning (e.g., as item or order numbers). For other use cases, we recommend the following:

  • For technical primary key fields, you can use the data element UUID for example (which has base type RAW(16)) rather than NUMC. UUID keys enable managed early numbering, meaning the RAP framework generates them automatically in the BDEF and no custom numbering logic is needed. In unmanaged BOs or classic ABAP, UUIDs can be generated via CL_SYSTEM_UUID directly, while in ABAP Cloud/BTP you can use the XCO library as well.
  • For counters or internal sequences, actual numeric types such as abap.int4 should be used instead.
  • For fiscal years or posting periods, we recommend using a DATN column instead. If for some reason this is not possible, the more suitable alternative would be using dedicated data elements or CDS types which have NUMC as their base type, but feature proper conversion exits as well. For data elements they can be directly included in the domain, while in CDS types they are added via annotation AbapCatalog.typeSpec.conversionExit.
  • For digit sequences such as postal codes, abap.char is the more future-proof choice in case letters need to be added later.
  • Any field which is exposed in OData should have also a CHAR-type instead of NUMC to avoid the need for extra handling of the leading zeros.

Lastly, some character-like types are also no longer supported in CDS table entities:

Deprecated types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.lchr

c

The type abap.clnt is known for being used solely for client fields. However, since we no longer denote client fields explicitly, we chose to no longer support this type either to avoid confusion.

The issue with abap.lchr is that this type requires the field length to be declared as an additional INT-field right before the LCHR, which is already impractical. Additionally, there can be only one such LCHR field in a table, and both the INT- and LCHR fields have to be the last columns at the end of the table. Since this type has no advantages on the database, we recommend using abap.string or abap.sstring instead, which map to proper LOB column types in HANA and get the job done just as well.


Byte-like types

With regards to byte-like types, the following are supported in CDS table entities:

The type abap.rawstring, just like abap.string, is also considered to have unlimited length and has no allowed length component other than abap.rawstring(0). Moreover, it is nullable as well, requiring the null keyword.

The type abap.lraw however is deprecated, since it poses a similar problem as abap.lchr. It can be replaced in the same fashion with abap.raw or abap.rawstring.

Currency and quantity types

One of the most frequent use cases is denoting currency and quantity fields. All the currency and quantity types you are already familiar with are supported in CDS table entities and mapped as follows:

Date and time

For date and time formats, we decided to only support the more modern types abap.datn, abap.timn and abap.utclong/abap.utcl, while deprecating the „old“ types abap.dats, abap.tims and abap.accp. An overview can be seen below:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

This change mainly stems from architectural reasons: the old types are character-like formats with ABAP-specific semantics that don't cleanly translate to proper database column types. A DATS-field simply contains a character in format 'YYYYMMDD', but the values are not enforced. A DATN-field on the other hand contains a true DATE-type value, meaning the column is enforced to have a valid date on the database. A similar principle can be applied to TIMS/TIMN: while TIMS is mapped to NVARCHAR, TIMN represents a true time value on the database as well. One example use case where this comes in handy is when calculating date and time directly on the database within an AMDP procedure. CDS table entities are designed to have real, native database columns, so therefore the old character-like types are no longer supported.

What time is it, actually? - Some remarks on time zones and timestamp conversions

A lot of users are still familiar with the legacy conversion functions CONVERT_DATE_TO_TIMESTAMP, GET_CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, etc. These functions combine the system date and time (sy-datum and sy-uzeit) and reconstruct a timestamp in UTC format. This is a common pitfall, since the resulting value does not represent the time in the „true“ UTC time zone, but instead the local system time in the respective „utclong“ format. The built-in type abap.utclong on the other hand maps to a real HANA TIMESTAMP column, meaning HANA's own SQL timestamp functions (ADD_SECONDS, SECONDS_BETWEEN, etc.) work directly on it without format conversion overhead. Furthermore, the UTCL_* family of CDS functions (UTCL_CURRENT, UTCL_ADD_SECONDS, UTCL_SECONDS_BETWEEN) only work on utclong-typed fields, whereas the older TSTMP_* functions only work on TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPL (which are data elements with base type decimal).

There is one very practical question that still remains here: if a user wants to store an event time, should they use UTCLONG alone, or DATN+TIMN+UTCLONG?

Our recommendation is to use utclong as the primary timestamp. DATN and TIMN are for cases where the date or time-of-day alone has independent business meaning. We also strongly discourage reconstructing timestamps from date and time in the same way it had been done with dats and tims in the past. Timestamps are stored in UTC, and recreating this antipattern would lose the time zone safety in the process.


Geodata types

The HANA type ST_GEOMETRY, which is used to store geometric data in EWKB representation, is supported in both classic tables and CDS table entities via the type abap.geom_ewkb:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.geom_ewkb

GEOM_EWKB

xstring

ST_GEOMETRY

This type has some special properties: it has no length, and it requires the specification of spatial reference system identifier (SRS ID or SRID). A spatial reference system defines the coordinate framework used to describe positions on earth, e.g., specifying the origin point, axis directions and units of measurement. The SRID is set via the field annotation AbapCatalog.geo.spatialRefSystem: '<SRID>, the default value being SRID=0. With a given SRS ID for a geodata column, the SRS ID is fixed at table creation. All records need to have this SRS ID, and it cannot be changed later. 
For CDS table entities on particular, we officially support SRID = NULL, which also changes the behavior compared to classic tables. If NULL is set as SRID, the SRS is not fixed at table creation anymore, meaning different values can be inserted later. This option however comes at the expense of performance. Furthermore, this type cannot be used for key fields regardless of whether the SRID is NULL or not.
Just like abap.string and abap.rawstring, abap.geom.ewkb is a nullable type and requires the null keyword as well.

This already concludes the first part on field definitions, builtin-types and type mappings. The next part of this series is going to cover data elements, CDS simple types and enumerations, so stay tuned!
