entry.title: Calling On-Premise Systems from Go on SAP BTP: Bindings, Tunnels and Destinations
entry.content:
The problem

While building a small Go service on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, that had to reach two things behind an SAP Cloud Connector: an SFTP server and an OData v2 service. Before any business logic, there were three small problems to solve:

  1. Where are my credentials? On Cloud Foundry they are in VCAP_SERVICES. On SAP BTP, Kyma runtime they are files in the pod.
  2. How do I get a TCP connection through the Connectivity service? Its SOCKS5 proxy uses a login method specific to SAP.
  3. How do I turn a Destination service entry into a client I can call? The destination describes the target, but you still have to apply it yourself.

Below is how each one was solved. I'm assuming you already know how to create and bind the Destination, Connectivity and Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA) service instances and map a virtual host in Cloud Connector.

1. Reading bindings without caring where you run

The code that reads credentials shouldn't change between Cloud Foundry and Kyma. I put both behind one small interface, with a detector that picks the right one at startup:

prov, err := auto.NewProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

cb, err := binding.Connectivity(prov, "") // proxy host and ports, client id/secret
db, err := binding.Destination(prov, "")  // Destination service URI and credentials

An empty name takes the first binding of that type; pass an instance name if you have several. Detection checks VCAP_SERVICES first, then SERVICE_BINDING_ROOT, then whether a /bindings directory exists.

2. A tunnel through the Connectivity service

The Connectivity service offers a SOCKS5 proxy. Instead of the usual username/password, it expects an SAP-specific authentication method (0x80) in which you send a JWT from XSUAA. The standard library and golang.org/x/net/proxy don't implement it, so I wrote it.

You give the dialer a token source (client-credentials tokens, cached until shortly before they expire) and the proxy details from the binding:

connSrc := xsuaa.NewClientCredentialsSource(xsuaa.Config{
    ClientID:     cb.ClientID,
    ClientSecret: cb.ClientSecret,
    TokenURL:     cb.TokenServiceURL + "/oauth/token",
})

dialer := connectivity.NewDialer(connectivity.Config{
    ProxyHost:   cb.OnpremiseProxyHost,
    ProxyPort:   cb.OnpremiseProxySocks5Port,
    TokenSource: connSrc,
})

conn, err := dialer.Dial(ctx, "internal-sftp.corp", 22, "")

The host and port must match a virtual mapping in Cloud Connector; the last argument is the Cloud Connector location ID (empty means the default location). You get back a plain net.Conn, so SSH, TLS or anything else can run on top.

Gotcha: when a dial fails, the error is a *connectivity.StageError that says whether it failed at dial, greeting, auth or connect. That tells you quickly whether to look at the token or at Cloud Connector access control.

For SFTP I also added sshclient.Dial, a thin wrapper that builds the SSH config from the destination and retries handshake failures with backoff.

3. From a Destination to a working HTTP client

Destination lookups use the same token pattern, built from the destination binding:

destSrc := xsuaa.NewClientCredentialsSource(xsuaa.Config{
    ClientID:     db.ClientID,
    ClientSecret: db.ClientSecret,
    TokenURL:     db.TokenServiceURL + "/oauth/token",
})
destClient := destination.NewClient(db.URI, destSrc, nil)

dest, err := destClient.Find(ctx, "MY_HTTP_DEST")

Then httpclient.New turns the destination into an *http.Client that applies its authentication and, for OnPremise destinations, routes through the Connectivity service's HTTP proxy:

cfg := httpclient.Config{}
if strings.EqualFold(dest.ProxyType, "OnPremise") {
    cfg.HTTPProxy = &httpclient.HTTPProxyConfig{Binding: cb}
}
client, baseURL, err := httpclient.New(dest, cfg)

resp, err := client.Get(baseURL + "/sap/opu/odata/sap/MY_SERVICE/Items?$top=5")

Gotcha: OData v2 writes need an X-CSRF-Token that is tied to a session cookie. The client keeps a cookie jar for that, and a helper fetches the token:

csrf, err := httpclient.FetchCSRF(ctx, client, baseURL+"/")
req.Header.Set("X-CSRF-Token", csrf) // then client.Do(req) for the POST

What it doesn't do

  • Client-credentials only. No principal propagation or user token exchange; everything runs as your service binding's technical client.
  • Secret-based bindings only. Bindings that use X.509 certificates instead of a client secret aren't handled.
  • sshclientskips SSH host-key checking by default. You can pass your own HostKeyCallback, and in anything beyond a demo you should.
  • Tested against fakes. The unit tests use local fake proxies and httptest servers, not a real Connectivity service, Destination service or Cloud Connector. [Author: state exactly what you have run end to end, e.g. whether you ran the Kyma path on a real cluster.]
  • Not an SAP product. It's an independent project, not provided or endorsed by SAP. It relies on service behaviour as I understood it from SAP's documentation and from observation, so check it against the current documentation for your landscape.

Quick start

The repository has three runnable Cloud Foundry examples (examples/sftp-count, examples/sftp-sshclient, examples/http-odata), each with a manifest and README. For the OData one:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa
cf create-service connectivity lite my-connectivity
cf create-service destination lite my-destination

cd examples/http-odata
cf push
curl "https://<app-route>/odata?destination=MY_HTTP_DEST&path=/Items?%24top=5"

It needs Go 1.25 or later. Apart from sshclient, which uses golang.org/x/crypto, the packages use only the standard library, and there are no SAP-published Go dependencies. On my machine (Go 1.25.10, macOS arm64) go test -cover reports between about 70% and 94% statement coverage per module; that measures what the fakes exercise, not behaviour against real systems.

It's open source under the Apache License 2.0 at https://github.com/bluefunda/btp-go, with API docs at https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/bluefunda/btp-go. Several modules are still v0.x, so expect the API to change. Corrections are welcome, especially from anyone who has seen the Connectivity proxy behave differently in another landscape or on Kyma.

entry.title: Working on SAP ECC-to-S/4HANA Remediation as a Functional Consultant with KTern.AI CodeGenie
entry.content:
Why the Remediation Was Needed

During a SAP remediation project, I worked on custom ABAP program analysis and remediation with the help of KTern.AI CodeGenie.

The remediation was triggered by an organizational-structure reassignment in the client's environment. Several custom programs relied on hard-coded organizational values, which needed to be addressed as part of the change.

Instead of simply replacing the old values with new hard-coded values, the project used a custom Z table. The program name and an ID were used to identify the relevant variable, and its value was maintained in the table. The program could then retrieve the required value instead of relying on a value embedded directly in the source code.

This approach made the remediation more maintainable because future changes to the relevant values could be handled through table maintenance rather than requiring another source-code modification for every affected value.

What made this project particularly interesting to me was my role. I was working as a SAP functional consultant, but the remediation required me to investigate technical issues, understand ABAP programs, and work with code changes. This was where CodeGenie became particularly useful.

Setting Up KTern.AI CodeGenie in VS Code

We used KTern.AI CodeGenie through Visual Studio Code. The setup involved installing the relevant KTern extensions, configuring an MCP server to connect to the SAP system, and adding the custom-code remediation skill required for the work.

Once the connection and skill were configured, we could interact with CodeGenie using natural language. We could ask it to retrieve and explain source code, trace program execution, identify relevant database tables, and investigate specific issues.

Another detail I noticed was that CodeGenie created a dedicated folder for each chat. This helped keep the artifacts associated with individual sessions organized.

How I Used CodeGenie as a Functional Consultant

As a functional consultant, I am more accustomed to working with business processes, configuration, master data, and functional issues than to spending all my time analyzing ABAP code.

During this project, I needed to understand existing custom programs, investigate why certain reports were failing, identify dependencies, and work through technical remediation.

CodeGenie helped bridge the gap between functional understanding and technical implementation.

For example, I could ask it to explain the purpose of a program, identify the tables it used, trace the execution flow, and explain how different parts of the code worked together. When an error occurred, I could ask it to investigate the underlying cause instead of relying only on the error message.

When a code change was required, I could discuss the intended behavior with CodeGenie, clarify the expected flow, and review the updated code it generated.

This made working on technical remediation much more approachable for me as a functional consultant. It did not eliminate the need to understand the business process or validate the changes, but it made technical investigation easier and helped me work more confidently with custom ABAP programs.

Working Through Several SAP Programs Over a Couple of Months

Across seven sessions spanning a couple of months, I used CodeGenie to investigate and work with several custom SAP programs. These covered purchasing, pricing, GST reporting, physical inventory, warehouse management, scheduling agreements, and BOM reporting.

The programs had different purposes and levels of complexity. Some generated reports, while others uploaded data or updated business documents.

Rather than listing every program individually, I want to highlight the types of work CodeGenie helped me with.

Understanding Existing Program Logic

Some programs contained multiple includes, custom function modules, or class dependencies. Understanding the complete execution flow required looking beyond a single source file.

CodeGenie retrieved and analyzed the source and helped explain how the different components worked together. It traced flows such as file upload, input validation, authorization checks, database updates, and ALV output generation.

For a GST sales register, it also helped explain the output columns and how the report handled different tax types and special business scenarios.

This was useful because understanding what an existing program was doing was an important first step before deciding what needed to change.

Understanding Existing Technical Changes

The programs contained various technical changes and dependencies that needed to be understood before further remediation.

CodeGenie helped explain database access patterns, replacements involving CDS views and compatibility views, and the handling of hard-coded values.

For me, this made it easier to understand the existing implementation and identify the areas that needed further investigation.

A Practical Example: Remediating a Cycle Count Report

One of the clearest examples from my experience involved a cycle count overview report that consolidated physical inventory information from Materials Management (MM) and Warehouse Management (WM).

During testing, we encountered an issue related to the fiscal year variant. A value was hard-coded in the program, but that value was not configured for the relevant year in the test system.

CodeGenie helped investigate the issue and presented two possible approaches: correcting the SAP configuration or changing the code. We chose the code-remediation approach.

CodeGenie investigated the relationship between the plant, valuation area, company code, and fiscal year variant. It also queried the live SAP system to verify the relevant values.

After checking the lookup chain, the remediation replaced five hard-coded fiscal year variant literals with dynamic derivation.

The change was then applied under a transport request, with the relevant locking, activation, and system-update steps.

What I found valuable was the investigation that happened before the code change. The issue was not approached simply as a request to replace a hard-coded value. The relevant organizational relationships and system values were examined to determine how the program should derive the required value.

As a functional consultant, this was a useful example of how I could participate in technical remediation with support from an AI coding agent while still reviewing the proposed solution.

Code Changes Were Only One Part of the Work

The development workflow involved more than asking CodeGenie to rewrite a program.

We first identified an object flagged as requiring remediation. We then asked CodeGenie to analyze the program and explain the issue. Once we understood the existing flow, we discussed the required changes and clarified the intended behavior.

CodeGenie could then make the proposed changes and display the updated code for review.

We checked whether the code contained all the changes discussed and whether the implementation matched the intended approach. If we were satisfied, we could approve the changes and have CodeGenie push the code to the SAP system through a transport request (TR).

This review step was important. We did not simply accept every generated change without checking it. We needed to understand the requirement and confirm that the proposed implementation reflected what had been agreed.

The workflow helped connect program analysis, code changes, review, and transport handling in one process.

Testing: Finding the Right Data Was Not Always Easy

One of the biggest practical challenges was finding suitable test data.

CodeGenie could suggest test cases and query the SAP system for relevant data. However, the first suggested test cases did not always produce the expected output. In some cases, executing the program returned no data.

When this happened, we asked CodeGenie to investigate possible master-data and configuration issues. Through multiple exchanges, we eventually identified working test data for the scenarios we were investigating.

Some of the issues encountered included:

  • Customer-material information records missing from the test system.

  • No suitable bills of material available for the selected materials.

  • Sales organizations in the test system differing from those used in production.

  • Configuration combinations missing from custom configuration tables.

  • Selection-screen parameters preventing the expected BOM from being found.

  • Missing descriptions in master data resulting in blank fields in exported output.

These issues highlighted an important distinction between changing code and validating its behavior. Even when the program logic is understood, testing can depend on suitable master data, configuration, organizational assignments, and input values.

For example, while testing a BOM explosion report, the BOM Application selection parameter contributed to a NO_SUITABLE_BOM_FOUND error. Clearing that field allowed the program to execute successfully and generate the expected CSV output. Reviewing the result also revealed a missing OEM device description in the relevant master data.

This was a useful reminder that successful execution does not automatically mean the output is complete or correct.

CodeGenie helped us investigate these issues, but the process was iterative. Its initial test suggestions were not always sufficient, and we had to ask further questions and investigate the underlying data and configuration before arriving at a working scenario.

For me, this was an important practical lesson: AI-assisted testing still requires careful investigation when the test environment does not contain the data or configuration needed for a scenario.

No-Data Issues and Variant Remediation

Apart from source-code remediation, the work also involved investigating reports that returned no data and programs whose variants did not produce the expected results.

A no-data issue occurs when a report is expected to return output based on available master data, but execution produces an empty screen or no results. The challenge is to determine whether the cause lies in the program logic, selection criteria, master data, configuration, or another dependency.

Variants introduce a related challenge. A program may execute successfully, but a particular variant may not retrieve the expected data. The variant and the way its selection parameters interact with the underlying program logic need to be investigated.

CodeGenie helped us analyze the program behavior and investigate these issues. As with the testing examples, reaching the correct conclusion sometimes required multiple exchanges and checking the available system data.

These scenarios reinforced that remediation is not always about syntax or replacing a hard-coded value. Understanding why a program does not return the expected result is often just as important as making the code change itself.

What I Took Away from the Experience

Across these sessions, I found CodeGenie useful for several connected activities:

  • Understanding existing ABAP programs and their execution flows.

  • Investigating code dependencies across includes, function modules, and classes.

  • Understanding existing technical changes and hard-coded values.

  • Querying SAP data to investigate errors and identify suitable test data.

  • Finding potential master-data and configuration gaps.

  • Implementing agreed code changes and supporting the review and transport workflow.

The most important benefit for me was how it helped me approach technical remediation as a functional consultant. I could use my understanding of the business process and SAP functionality while relying on CodeGenie to help investigate the technical implementation.

At the same time, the experience showed that AI assistance does not eliminate the need for technical judgment. The requirements still need to be clear, code changes need to be reviewed, and unsuccessful tests need to be investigated rather than assumed to be correct.

The most effective workflow was not simply asking CodeGenie to fix a program. It was using it to understand the issue, discuss the required approach, investigate relevant SAP data, review the resulting changes, and work through testing problems until we could identify a suitable scenario.

For SAP functional consultants who need to work with custom ABAP programs, this kind of assistance can make technical remediation more approachable.

My main takeaway is that KTern.AI CodeGenie can be a useful partner in SAP remediation—not as a replacement for functional knowledge or human review, but as a tool that helps connect functional understanding with technical investigation and implementation.

entry.title: How to do achieve auto Nested packing in EWM
entry.content:
In SAP EWM, a Handling Unit (HU) is a physical unit that combines packaging material and the products packed inside it. Nested Handling Units allow us to create a hierarchy of packaging, where one HU is packed inside another HU.

For example, individual products can be packed into cartons, multiple cartons can be placed on a pallet, and multiple pallets can be loaded onto a truck or another transport unit, depending on the warehouse process.

The main advantage is that EWM can manage the packaging hierarchy and the stock contained within it. Instead of handling every individual carton separately, warehouse operators can move, scan, pick, and track a larger packaging unit while retaining visibility into its contents.

Auto nested packing lets SAP EWM build a full packing hierarchy, such as bottles in cartons and cartons on a pallet, the moment an inbound delivery is created. Warehouse Operator does have to pack manually in EWM, and the system creates every handling unit (HU) for us.

This post uses a simple example. We pack 12 bottles of bottles into one carton, then 5 cartons onto one pallet:

  • 1 carton = 12 bottles
  • 1 pallet = 5 cartons = 60 bottles

Configuration:

  1. Packaging Specifications.

 

1.1 Define the number range for packaging specifications.

 

1.2 Define general packaging specification parameters.

1.3 Define the packaging specification group.

1.4 Maintain the master data for packaging specifications. The level set it uses is defined in step 2.3.

2. Maintain the structure of the packaging specification:

2.1 Define level types. Here you define the packing elements, such as pallet and carton. Set both to HU, so each generates its own HU number and is packed into the other.

2.2 Define element types. Assign a type to each element above. The packing materials act as main or auxiliary packing material.

2.3 Define the level set. Combine all packaging elements and mark whether each one is a packing material. Set the sequence: carton first, then pallet. Assign each level to the main packing element type.

 

 

 

2.4 Define packaging material types.

2.5 Assign the packaging material type to the element type.

3. Determine packaging specifications. Create the determination procedure if you need it.

4. Assign the procedure to the document type, here the inbound delivery document type, so the system looks for a specification when a delivery is created.

 

 

 

5. Master Data

Create the packaging specification for your product

Create the specification itself in transaction /SCWM/PACKSPEC.

1. Create the packaging specification and its condition record for the product. Enter a description and select the packaging specification group.

2. Open the detail view and create the conditions by selecting the condition type.

3. Set up the carton level. Double-click the carton, enter a target quantity of 12 and select HU Creation. The system then creates a HU for the carton as well as for the packing material.

4. Set up the pallet level the same way. Target quantity is 5, because each pallet holds 5 cartons (60 bottles). HU Creation makes the system create a HU for the pallet after the carton.

5. Add the product to the content. Right-click Content and add the product. Open the content, click the product and enter a quantity of 1.

6. Activate and save the specification.

 

The result in the inbound delivery

Create an inbound delivery for 60 bottles. If packing does not come from ECC, EWM packs automatically using the specification. It creates 6 HUs: 5 cartons and 1 pallet, with the 60 bottles in the 5 cartons and the 5 cartons on the pallet.

 

The delivery shows the highest level, the pallet. To see the full structure, select Display HU, which lists the pallet and the cartons packed into it.

Conclusion

Nested Handling Units provide a structured way to manage multiple levels of packaging in SAP EWM. We can pack individual products into cartons, consolidate those cartons onto a pallet, and maintain visibility of the entire packaging hierarchy.

From an operational perspective, this can reduce repetitive scanning and handling, simplify pallet movements, improve packing accuracy, and support better visibility during staging, loading, and shipping.

The key benefit is that we can manage the physical movement of a larger unit without losing track of the smaller units and products packed inside it.

entry.content:
Hello SAP Community! 👋

In this blog post, I would like to share my hands-on experience building my first application using the SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

As part of my learning journey, I developed a simple Student Management Application using Managed RAP, ABAP CDS View Entities, OData V2, and SAP Fiori Elements.

The main objective was to understand how the different RAP development artifacts work together to build a transactional application.

The application supports standard CRUD operations:

  • Create — Add new students.

  • Read — Display existing student records.

  • Update — Modify student information.

  • Delete — Remove student records.

In this tutorial, I'll explain each development step, share the code, and discuss some challenges I encountered.

My Personal Experience

I started this project with a simple Managed RAP application that supported basic CRUD operations.

As I continued practicing in Eclipse and testing the application with SAP Fiori Elements, I wanted to understand how RAP handles real business requirements.

One of the most useful parts of the project was implementing Draft Handling. I initially encountered an error because the draft persistence table was not configured correctly. After resolving it, I tested the application by creating a student, leaving the page without activating the record, and returning to find my draft still available.

I also enjoyed implementing the Approve Student action and seeing the student status change from NEW to APPROVED directly in Fiori.

Working through these steps helped me understand RAP much better than simply reading about its features.

AI disclosure: I used ChatGPT to help structure and draft parts of this article. The application development, troubleshooting, and testing described here were performed hands-on.

1. Application Architecture

Before starting the development, let's understand the main components of the application.

Our application consists of the following artifacts:

Artifact Object Name

Database TableZSTD_TABLE_DEMO
Interface CDS ViewZ_I_STD
Projection CDS ViewZ_C_STD
Base Behavior DefinitionZ_I_STD
Behavior PoolZBP_I_STD
Projection Behavior DefinitionZ_C_STD
Metadata ExtensionZ_C_STD
Service DefinitionZ_SD_STD
Service BindingOData V2 - UI

The database table stores the data, CDS Views define the data model and its projection, Behavior Definitions control transactional operations, and the service layer exposes the application to SAP Fiori.

2. Create the Database Table

Object Name: ZSTD_TABLE_DEMO

The first step is creating a database table to store student information.

In Eclipse ADT, create a new Database Table and add the following code:

@EndUserText.label : 'STUDENT TABLE'
@AbapCatalog.enhancement.category : #NOT_EXTENSIBLE
@AbapCatalog.tableCategory : #TRANSPARENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #C
@AbapCatalog.dataMaintenance : #ALLOWED

define table zstd_table_demo {

  key client       : abap.clnt not null;
  key rollno       : sysuuid_x16 not null;

  studentname      : abap.char(100);
  studentclass     : abap.char(2);
  studentage       : abap.numc(3);
  schoolname       : abap.char(150);

}

Explanation

The table contains student information such as Name, Class, Age, and School Name.

The rollno field uses sysuuid_x16 as the primary key.

This allows us to use automatic UUID generation through the RAP Managed Runtime.

Note: This learning example uses delivery class #C. For a typical transactional application that stores business data, #A is generally more appropriate.

Activate the table using Ctrl + F3.

3. Create the Interface CDS View

Object Name: Z_I_STD

Next, we create the Interface CDS View.

This view represents the underlying data model of our RAP Business Object.

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'BASIC VIEW FOR STD'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true

define root view entity Z_I_STD
  as select from zstd_table_demo
{
  key rollno       as Rollno,
      studentname  as Studentname,
      studentclass as Studentclass,
      studentage   as Studentage,
      schoolname   as Schoolname
}

Explanation

The Interface CDS View reads data from the database table and defines the entity structure.

We use define root view entity because this is the root entity of our RAP Business Object.

The Rollno field is defined as the key.

The CDS View can also be used to define associations and compositions in more advanced RAP applications.

Key Learning: The Interface CDS View defines the core data model.

4. Create the Projection CDS View

Object Name: Z_C_STD

The next step is creating a Projection CDS View based on our Interface CDS View.

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'CONSUMPTION VIEW FOR STD'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
@Metadata.allowExtensions: true

define root view entity Z_C_STD
  as projection on Z_I_STD
{
  key Rollno,
      Studentname,
      Studentclass,
      Studentage,
      Schoolname
}

Explanation

The Projection CDS View defines which fields are exposed to service consumers.

In this example, we expose all the fields from our Interface CDS View.

However, in real applications, we can expose only selected fields.

For example, an administrator and a teacher could use different projection views built on the same underlying business object.

Important Difference:

  • Interface CDS View: Defines the underlying data model.

  • Projection CDS View: Defines the projected data available to consumers.

  • Metadata Extension: Controls how the data appears in Fiori.

The annotation @Metadata.allowExtensions: true enables metadata extensions for our projection.

5. Create the Base Behavior Definition

Behavior Definition for: Z_I_STD

Now we define the transactional behavior of our application.

Since we are using Managed RAP, the RAP framework handles standard database persistence operations automatically.

managed implementation in class zbp_i_std unique;
strict ( 2 );

define behavior for Z_I_STD alias _studentdetail
persistent table zstd_table_demo
lock master
authorization master ( instance )
{
  create;
  update;
  delete;

  field ( readonly, numbering : managed ) Rollno;
}

Explanation

Let's understand the important statements.

Managed Implementation

The RAP framework handles the standard Create, Update, and Delete persistence operations.

Persistent Table

The statement persistent table zstd_table_demo defines where our business object data is stored.

Lock Master

Defines the root entity as the lock master.

Authorization Master

Enables instance-level authorization control, which requires a corresponding implementation in the behavior pool.

Managed Numbering

field ( readonly, numbering : managed ) Rollno;

This enables automatic UUID generation.

We do not need to manually generate the student UUID during creation.

6. Create the Behavior Implementation Class

Object Name: ZBP_I_STD

The Behavior Pool contains custom implementation logic required by the RAP Business Object.

In Managed RAP, we do not need to manually implement standard database CRUD persistence.

However, we declared instance authorization in the Base Behavior Definition, so we must provide the corresponding authorization handler.

Global Behavior Pool Class

CLASS zbp_i_std DEFINITION
  PUBLIC
  ABSTRACT
  FINAL
  FOR BEHAVIOR OF Z_I_STD.

ENDCLASS.

CLASS zbp_i_std IMPLEMENTATION.

ENDCLASS.

Local Handler Class

In the Behavior Pool's Local Types, the instance authorization method can be implemented as follows:

CLASS lhc_Student DEFINITION
  INHERITING FROM cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  PRIVATE SECTION.

    METHODS get_instance_authorizations
      FOR INSTANCE AUTHORIZATION
      IMPORTING keys
      REQUEST requested_authorizations
      FOR _studentdetail
      RESULT result.

ENDCLASS.

CLASS lhc_Student IMPLEMENTATION.

  METHOD get_instance_authorizations.

    result = VALUE #(
      FOR key IN keys
      (
        %tky    = key-%tky
        %update = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
        %delete = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
      )
    ).

  ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS.

Explanation

The method get_instance_authorizations determines whether operations are authorized for specific business object instances.

In this simplified learning example, Update and Delete operations are allowed without checking a real authorization object.

Important: This permissive implementation is for demonstration only. A productive application must implement appropriate authorization checks. Use the handler declarations generated by ADT if they differ from this example.

7. Create the Projection Behavior Definition

Behavior Definition for: Z_C_STD

After defining the Base Behavior, we create the Projection Behavior Definition.

projection;
strict ( 2 );

define behavior for Z_C_STD alias _studentdetail
{
  use create;
  use update;
  use delete;
}

Explanation

The Base Behavior Definition defines the operations supported by the Business Object.

The Projection Behavior Definition exposes selected operations to consumers.

For example:

  • create; in the Base BDEF defines the Create operation.

  • use create; in the Projection BDEF exposes that operation.

No separate behavior implementation class is required for these projected standard operations.

8. Create the Metadata Extension

Metadata Extension for: Z_C_STD

Now we define how our application should look in SAP Fiori Elements.

Instead of placing UI annotations directly in the CDS View, we use a Metadata Extension.

@Metadata.layer: #CORE

annotate entity Z_C_STD with
{
  @UI.facet: [{
    type: #IDENTIFICATION_REFERENCE,
    position: 1,
    label: 'STUDENT DETAIL'
  }]

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 1, label: 'Student ID' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 1, label: 'Student ID' }]
  Rollno;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 2, label: 'Student name' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 2, label: 'Student name' }]
  Studentname;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 3, label: 'Student Class' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 3, label: 'Student Class' }]
  Studentclass;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 4, label: 'Student Age' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 4, label: 'Student Age' }]
  Studentage;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 5, label: 'School name' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 5, label: 'School name' }]
  Schoolname;
}

Explanation

The most important UI annotations in this example are:

@UI.lineItem

Defines the fields displayed as columns in the Fiori List Report.

@UI.identification

Defines the fields displayed in the identification section of the Object Page.

@UI.facet

Defines sections within the Object Page.

Using Metadata Extensions helps separate the UI design from the underlying business data model.

9. Create the Service Definition

Object Name: Z_SD_STD

After completing the CDS Views and Behavior Definitions, we create a Service Definition.

@EndUserText.label: 'SERVICE DEFINITION FOR STD'

define service Z_SD_STD {
  expose Z_C_STD;
}

Explanation

The Service Definition identifies which CDS entity will be exposed to external consumers.

Here, we expose the Projection CDS View Z_C_STD.

This keeps the service focused on the consumption model rather than exposing the underlying interface entity directly.

10. Create the Service Binding

Service Binding: Z_UI_STD_O2

The final development step is creating a Service Binding.

In Eclipse ADT:

  1. Right-click the package and create a new Service Binding.

  2. Enter the name Z_UI_STD_O2.

  3. Select the Service Definition Z_SD_STD.

  4. Choose OData V2 - UI as the binding type.

  5. Activate the Service Binding.

  6. Publish the service using the available publishing option.

  7. Select the exposed entity and launch the Fiori Elements Preview.

The availability of OData binding types depends on the backend release.

Explanation

The Service Definition determines what is exposed.

The Service Binding determines how the service is exposed through the selected OData protocol.

In this example, we used OData V2 - UI to generate a SAP Fiori Elements application preview.

11. Testing the Application

After launching the Fiori Elements Preview, the Student Management application displayed the student fields configured in the Metadata Extension.

I created student records and verified that the generated UUIDs were assigned automatically.

The List Report successfully displayed the persisted student data.

The Behavior Definition also exposes Update and Delete operations. These should be tested individually to verify the complete CRUD scenario.

12. Challenges and Troubleshooting

During development, I encountered two interesting issues.

Challenge 1 — Fiori Preview Connectivity

Initially, the Fiori Elements Preview was not accessible because the generated service URL used a hostname and port that were not reachable from my environment.

To investigate the problem, I checked:

  • SMICM — HTTP and HTTPS services.

  • SICF — ICF service activation.

  • HTTPURLLOC — URL generation configuration.

  • Network connectivity to the SAP application server.

After identifying a working HTTPS endpoint, I was able to launch the application preview.

This experience highlighted the importance of SAP system connectivity and proper HTTP/HTTPS configuration.

Challenge 2 — Runtime Error During Create

When I initially tried creating a student, the application returned:

RAISE_SHORTDUMP

I opened transaction ST22 and found the following error:

CX_RAP_HANDLER_NOT_IMPLEMENTED

Handler not implemented
Method: INSTANCE_AUTHORIZATION

The reason was that I had declared:

authorization master ( instance )

But I had not implemented the corresponding authorization handler.

After implementing get_instance_authorizations in the Behavior Pool, the missing-handler error was resolved, and student creation worked successfully.

Key Learning

If we declare authorization handling in a RAP Behavior Definition, we must implement the required authorization methods.

ST22 is a valuable tool for investigating backend runtime errors during RAP development.

13. What I Learned

Building this application helped me understand several important SAP RAP concepts:

  1. How to create persistent tables using ABAP Dictionary DDL.

  2. The purpose of Interface and Projection CDS View Entities.

  3. How Managed RAP handles standard transactional persistence.

  4. How Behavior Definitions define supported operations.

  5. How Behavior Pools implement custom behavior and authorization.

  6. How Metadata Extensions configure SAP Fiori Elements applications.

  7. How Service Definitions and Service Bindings expose OData services.

  8. How to investigate runtime issues using SAP diagnostic tools.

Conclusion

Building my first SAP RAP Student Management Application was a valuable hands-on learning experience.

It helped me understand how the different components of the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model work together to deliver an OData-based transactional application.

Starting from a database table, I built a Managed RAP Business Object, exposed it through an OData V2 service, and successfully displayed and created student records using SAP Fiori Elements.

entry.title: Reusing Existing Specifications in SAP EHS Product Compliance Using SUBUPD and CODUPD User Exits
entry.content:
Introduction

In SAP EHS Product Compliance for Discrete Industries, Bill of Material (BOM) transfer processing can involve creating specifications and their corresponding compliance objects. However, in some business scenarios, an appropriate specification already exists for a material and should be reused instead of creating another one.

Creating duplicate specifications or compliance objects can lead to inconsistent data and unnecessary maintenance. This article explains one custom enhancement approach using the "LB_SUBUPD" and "LB_CODUPD" user exit categories to identify existing specifications, control specification creation, and align compliance-object data with the existing specification.

1. Configure the user exits

The user exits are configured in SAP Customizing under:

Product Safety and Stewardship > Product Compliance for Discrete Industries > Integration > Logistic Integration > Bill of Material Transfer > Manage User Exits

The standard configuration provides the following relevant user exit categories:

User exit category| Purpose

"LB_SUBUPD"| Edit specification data before it is saved in the database

"LB_CODUPD"| Update compliance-object data

In this implementation, custom function modules are assigned to these categories

The implementation follows the interface of the corresponding standard template function modules. The exact interface and processing sequence should be verified against the SAP release and configuration in use.

2. SUBUPD: Identify and reuse an existing specification

The "LB_SUBUPD" exit is used to check whether an existing specification can be reused during BOM transfer processing.

Step 1: Restrict processing to the relevant scenarios

The custom logic processes the "BB_HEAD_CR" and "BB_COMP_CR" scenarios. Other scenarios are ignored.

Step 2: Identify the material

The material number is obtained from the material-join data when available. Otherwise, the material number from the extended material structure is used.

Step 3: Find an existing specification

The lookup logic supports two flows.

- Material and supplier flow:

When supplier information is available, the logic searches the "ESTRI" identification records for a specification associated with both the material number and supplier.

- Material-only flow:

When supplier information is not available, the logic searches "ESTMJ" for material-to-specification assignments and checks "ESTRH" for a corresponding specification that has not been marked for deletion.

This distinction is important because the correct specification may depend on the supplier as well as the material.

Step 4: Validate the existing specification

After identifying a candidate specification, the logic checks the number of active specification-header records associated with the selected "RECNROOT".

If multiple records are found, the enhancement sets the error flag and returns a custom error message. This prevents processing from continuing with an ambiguous candidate.

The logic then reads the specification identifier ("SUBID") from "ESTRH", considering the validity date and deletion and parking indicators.

If no valid specification is found, the function module returns without applying the reuse logic.

Step 5: Control new specification creation

When a valid specification is found, the enhancement sets the cancellation flag and activates a custom processing flag. The intention is to prevent the normal creation flow from generating another specification for the same scenario.

The code also checks "EHPRCD_COD_ROOT" for an existing compliance object associated with the specification identifier and sets the cancellation flag when a matching record is found.

Finally, the logic prepares the identification data in "XT_IDENT" using the existing specification's identification records.

Key point: "SUBUPD" identifies a reusable specification and controls the specification-creation flow.

3. CODUPD: Align the compliance object with the existing specification

Finding an existing specification is only part of the solution. The compliance-object processing must also reference the appropriate specification and maintain the relevant material associations.

The "LB_CODUPD" implementation handles this part of the enhancement.

Step 1: Find the specification for the material

The lookup follows the supplier-linked or material-only flow, depending on the compliance object's supplier-part indicator.

For supplier-linked processing, the code searches "ESTRI" for a specification matching both the material and supplier.

For material-only processing, it uses "ESTMJ" and "ESTRH" to identify a corresponding specification.

Step 2: Read the specification's material assignments

When a candidate specification is found, the function module calls "C1F2_SUBSTANCES_READ" to read the specification data and its material-join information.

The returned specification identifier ("SUBID") is compared with the compliance object's existing "SUBSTANCE_ID".

When they differ, the custom logic updates "CS_COD_ROOT_DATA-SUBSTANCE_ID" and records the changed field in "CT_CHANGED_FIELDS_ROOT".

The implementation also prepares a success message containing the specification identifier and material number.

Step 3: Reuse an existing compliance object

The enhancement calls "CL_EHPRC_COD_DATA_HELPER=>FIND_CO_BY_SPECIFICATION_ID" to check whether a compliance object already exists for the specification.

The logic handles the following outcomes:

- Multiple compliance objects found: report an error and stop the remaining processing.

- General lookup error: issue a warning and stop the remaining processing.

- Existing compliance object found: use its key when it differs from the compliance object's current key.

- No existing compliance object found: continue with the current key as the new-object case.

The purpose is to avoid creating unnecessary duplicate compliance objects for a specification that already has a corresponding object.

Step 4: Maintain the material associations

The code obtains the compliance object's root node and its associated material node through the BOPF-based ENA framework.

It then compares the materials associated with the specification against the materials already associated with the compliance object.

For other materials returned by the specification's material-join data, the enhancement checks whether a material association already exists. Missing associations are created, with new BOPF keys and the relevant parent and root keys.

The code should also contain cleanup logic to identify material associations that are no longer present in the specification's material-join data and delete them from the node.

This step is important when a specification contains multiple materials: updating the specification reference alone does not guarantee that every required material association is maintained.

4. How the two exits work together

The overall processing pattern is:

1. BOM transfer starts and invokes the configured specification-update exit.

2. "SUBUPD" identifies the material and searches for an existing specification.

3. The enhancement validates the candidate and controls whether new specification creation should proceed.

4. The compliance-object update exit identifies the relevant specification again for the current material and supplier context.

5. "CODUPD" aligns the compliance object's specification reference.

6. The enhancement looks for an existing compliance object for the specification and handles its key.

7. The material associations are checked and updated as required.

8. The resulting specification and compliance-object relationships are validated after processing.

The two exits serve different purposes. "SUBUPD" focuses on specification-side processing, whereas "CODUPD" focuses on compliance-object data and material associations. Both need to be consistent with the standard processing sequence.

5. Testing and troubleshooting

The following checks help validate this type of enhancement.

Existing specification

- Confirm the material number and supplier used by the lookup.

- Verify the relevant records in "ESTMJ", "ESTRH", and "ESTRI".

- Check deletion, parking, and validity-date conditions.

- Confirm that the selected specification is unambiguous.

Compliance object

- Check "EHPRCD_COD_ROOT" for the specification identifier.

- Verify whether an existing compliance object is reused or a new one is created.

- Check the material associations through the compliance object's root-material relationship.

- Confirm that no duplicate compliance objects or unintended material associations are introduced.

User-exit execution

- Verify the configured sequence and assigned function modules in Manage User Exits.

- Debug both exits to confirm the scenario, material, supplier, specification identifier, compliance-object key, and cancellation/error flags.

- Test header-material and component-material processing separately, including repeated calls and specifications associated with multiple materials.

If a consistency error occurs because a compliance object has no material association, inspect the compliance object's root-material association at the point of validation. The existence of a specification for a component does not, by itself, prove that the compliance object being validated has the required material association.

Conclusion

Reusing an existing specification during SAP EHS Product Compliance BOM transfer requires more than finding a matching specification identifier. The enhancement must also control the standard specification-creation flow, identify the appropriate compliance object, and maintain the material associations consistently.

Using "LB_SUBUPD" and "LB_CODUPD" provides two distinct extension points for implementing this approach. Careful validation of the user-exit sequence, specification lookup criteria, BOPF node handling, and duplicate-processing behavior is essential to prevent inconsistent compliance data.

entry.title: SAP Business AI Explained: The Components You Need to Know
entry.content:
SAP Business AI can look like a shopping list: Joule, Joule Work, Joule Studio, Business Data Cloud, Knowledge Graph, AI Agent Hub. This post explains what each piece does and how they fit together.

The Big Picture

SAP’s Business AI Platform is built on three pillars: Build, Contextualize and Reason, and Govern.

 

The Components in Plain Language

 

How They Work Together

A user states a goal in Joule Work. An Assistant picks the right Agents. The agents use the Knowledge Graph and Business Data Cloud for context and run inside the Autonomous Suite. The Agent Gateway enforces permissions at each step, and the AI Agent Hub keeps every agent visible and governed.

Why This Is Not a Chatbot

 

 

 

A Short Example (illustrative)

User types in Joule Work: “A key customer reported a damaged delivery. Check replacement stock and update the service case.”

 

 

The user never opens five applications. This scenario is my own illustration, not an SAP-documented use case. Both assistants are named in SAP’s Sapphire 2026 guide, but check their current availability before promising them to a customer.

Open by Design

Agents built in Joule Studio natively support the MCP and A2A protocols to work with third-party tools and agents. Customers are not locked into agents built only by SAP.

Why This Matter

  • Data and process readiness → grounding through Knowledge Graph and Business Data Cloud
  • Custom capability → Joule Studio (low-code) or pro-code agents on SAP BTP
  • Governance and risk → identity, Agent Gateway and AI Agent Hub
  • Adoption → moving users from “navigate screens” to “state goals”

AI quality is limited by data quality. A strong platform on weak master data gives weak results.

Key Takeaways

  • The platform rests on three pillars: Build, Contextualize and Reason, Govern.
  • Joule Work is what users see. Grounding and governance make it trustworthy.
  • Assistants coordinate, agents execute, and the gateway enforces permissions.
  • MCP and A2A keep the architecture open.
  • Clean data and clear process ownership matter as much as the technology.

Closing Thought

Before asking “Which Joule feature should we activate?”, ask: “Is our data, process ownership and governance ready for AI to act on our behalf?”

entry.title: Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome in SAP SuccessFactors Performance Management
entry.content:
Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome in SAP SuccessFactors Performance Management

By Nishanth Kumar Puttapaka  ·  SAP SuccessFactors 2H 2026

Why this rule scenario matters

With the 2H 2026 release, SAP SuccessFactors Performance Management can email the right people automatically when a form reaches a specific outcome. You no longer need someone to watch the form inbox or run reports to spot it.

The new Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome rule scenario checks a form each time it is routed to the next step. If the form meets your conditions, it sends an email built from a Document Generation template. Typical uses from SAP's own examples:

  • Notify a career coaching team when the manager's overall rating is below 3.
  • Notify a sales performance team when more than 50% of an employee's goals are rated "Below Expectations".
  • Notify talent management when a promotion recommendation checkbox is selected.

I configured this scenario recently for a probation review: HR records the probation result in a custom field on the form, and the employee is notified automatically when the result is "Confirmed". This post walks through the full setup, from the picklist and email templates to the rule itself and its assignment.

The feature is customer configured: nothing changes until you build and assign a rule. It requires the latest experience of Performance Management forms.

 

Figure 1. How the rule runs: the email goes out only when the routed form meets every condition

The rule is checked each time the form moves forward in the route map; saving the form alone never sends an email.

Prerequisites

Check these before building anything. A missing setting is the most common reason the rule options don't appear.

Area

What must be in place

Provisioning

Enable Generic Objects is selected (done by your implementation partner)

Employee Central

Employee Central is enabled, and Document Generation is enabled in Manage Employee Central Settings > Basic Settings

Performance Management Feature Settings

Enable the latest experience of Performance Management forms and Enable business rules for Performance Management are selected

Form template

Any form data you want in the email exists as custom fields in custom sections (up to 20 fields per rule)

Custom fields

Fields added through XML have an ekey starting with a letter; list fields have a distinct List Element's Value (elist-value) per option, such as 1, 2, 3

Picklist (optional)

A picklist with code PMEmailRecipients, only if you email external addresses or distribution lists

 

The administrator doing the setup needs these role-based permissions:

  • Manage System Properties > Performance Management Feature Settings
  • Manage Templates > Form Templates, and Comprehensive template configuration for PMv12
  • Manage Document Generation > Manage Document Template, and Manage Document Template Mapping
  • Metadata Framework > Configure Business Rules
  • Assign Rules in Talent > Assign Rules for Performance Management

If you don't see the Assign Rules for Performance Management permission, select Enable Performance Management access permission in Performance Management Feature Settings.

Step-by-step configuration

The setup has five parts, and their order matters: the rule can only reference fields, template groups and picklist values that already exist.

1. Prepare the form template

The rule reads values from the form, so the data you want to test or show in the email must be on the template.

  1. Add a custom section for the decision you want to act on (in my example, a "Review Decision" section with an "Outcome Status" list field that HR updates with the probation result).
  2. Add the custom fields inside it. Supported types for rule conditions are checkbox, list, integer, double, date and text.
  3. For a list field, give every option a different List Element's Value (elist-value), such as 1, 2, 3. Users never see these values, but the rule page needs them to tell the options apart.
  4. If you add fields through XML, start each ekey with a letter.
  5. Check the route map. The rule runs only when the form is routed forward to a route map step. Submitting inside an iterative or collaboration step does not trigger it.

Avoid renaming the template after you create the rule. An unassigned rule can no longer be assigned, and an assigned rule can no longer be edited until you restore the original name.

2. Create the PMEmailRecipients picklist (optional)

You need this picklist only to email external addresses or distribution lists. Internal users can be picked directly in the rule.

  1. Go to Admin Center > Picklist Center and create a new picklist.
  2. Set the code to exactly PMEmailRecipients.
  3. Add one value per recipient:
    • External Code: the email address or distribution list address, for example hr-team@yourcompany.com
    • Label: a readable name, for example "HR Shared Mailbox"
  4. Save. The labels then appear as choices in the rule's Get Email Recipients for Performance Management function.

3. Build the email templates in Document Generation

Create the template group

  1. Go to Admin Center > Document Generation - Manage Document Template.
  2. In Create New, choose Document Generation Group.
  3. Enter an ID, name and description. Set Category to Performance Management Rule-Based Emails, then save.

Create the template

  1. In Create New, choose Document Generation Template.
  2. Set Category to Performance Management Rule-Based Emails and Group to the group you just created.
  3. Write the email subject and body. Add placeholders as [[placeholderText]], for example [[EmployeeName]] or [[OutcomeStatus]].
  4. Save. Add more templates to the group if you need other languages.

Map the placeholders

  1. Go to Admin Center > Document Generation - Manage Document Template Mapping and choose the template.
  2. For Employee Central data of the form subject (department, location, job title), use Mapping Type = Direct and pick the Base Object and Target Field.
  3. For form data, use Mapping Type = Reference and pick a token. Standard tokens include Form Title, Form Due Date, Form Sender Name, Form Sender Comment, Employee Name and Signature. Custom Token 1 to 20 carry your custom section fields.
  4. Save.

Don't use the Email Recipient Name tokens if you also email external addresses or distribution lists: they work for internal users only.

4. Create the business rule

  1. Go to Admin Center > Configure Business Rules and choose Create New Rule.
  2. Expand Performance Management and choose Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome.
  3. Enter the Rule Name, Rule ID, Start Date and the Form Template, then choose Continue.
  4. Build the If conditions (see the walkthrough below).
  5. In Then, choose Execute and select Trigger Email Notification for Performance Management.
  6. Set the email template group, the recipients and any custom tokens, then save.

5. Assign the rule to a trigger

A saved rule does nothing until it is assigned.

  1. Go to Admin Center > Assign Rules in Talent and open the Performance Management tab.
  2. Select the form template.
  3. Under Rules Grouped by Triggers, add an entry in Form Routing to Next Step and select your rule.
  4. Use the arrows to order rules if there are several, then save. Each trigger takes up to five rules per template.

Walkthrough: a working rule

The rule below sends an email when the HR review step is completed and the probation result in the custom field is "Confirmed". Names and values are anonymised; the structure is exactly as configured.

 

Figure 2. The business rule in the Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome scenario (names anonymised)

Basic information. The rule is created for one form template. The Parameters panel shows the two read-only objects the rule can use: Context (System Context) and Form.

If: two conditions joined by AND.

  • Form.Route Map.Current Step is equal to HR Review. This limits the rule to one route map step. Without a step or role condition, the rule applies to every step and role.
  • Form.Form Section.Review Decision.Outcome Status.Value is equal to Confirmed. This reads a list field in a custom section. For a list field, pick the Value directly under the field name, not a Value nested under another Value.

Then: Trigger Email Notification for Performance Management.

  • Email Template Group: the Document Generation group holding the "Confirmed" email templates.
  • Email Recipients (Individuals/Distribution Lists, Any Users): left as Null here, because no external address or distribution list is needed.
  • Email Recipients (Individuals, Internal Only): uses Get Users for Performance Management with three users: a named HR business partner, Form.Subject User (the employee being reviewed) and one more named user.
  • Custom Token 1: mapped to the same Outcome Status field, so the email body can print the decision.

Other conditions you can use

  • The subject user's Employee Central data: Subject User > object > field, such as location, department or job title.
  • Overall ratings: manual, calculated and adjusted overall ratings, goal and competency summaries, and performance or potential ratings.
  • Text length: section comments or text fields, counted without rich-text HTML tags.
  • Rating counts or proportions: the Get Count of Ratings function, combined with Divide for a percentage.

Rating fields use -1972 for "unrated" and -1971 for "too new to rate". When you test for a rating below a number, also require it to be greater than 0, so these special values don't match.

The email template and what the employee receives

The template lives in the "Outcome - Confirmed" group that the rule points to. Its category is Performance Management Rule-Based Emails, and the body uses placeholders for the issue date, employee name, designation, employee ID and hire date.

 

Figure 3. The Document Generation email template in the Performance Management Rule-Based Emails category

When HR routes the form with the result set to "Confirmed", the employee receives the email below, with every placeholder filled from Employee Central and the form. The names and values shown are sample data.

 

Figure 4. The email received by the employee (sample data)

Recipients and workflow participants

This rule can reach people outside the route map. Route map participants (employee, manager, HR) already get the standard routing emails; this rule adds anyone else who needs to act on the outcome.

Two recipient parameters control who gets the email. Both are optional, but if both are empty no email is sent.

Parameter

Identifies people by

Who it can reach

How to fill it

Email language

Email Recipients (Individuals/Distribution Lists, Any Users)

Email address

Internal users, external users, distribution lists

Type addresses separated by semicolons, or use Get Email Recipients for Performance Management to pick from the PMEmailRecipients picklist

Default language template only

Email Recipients (Individuals, Internal Only)

User ID

Internal users only

Type user IDs separated by semicolons, or use Get Users for Performance Management to search and add users with the plus icon

Each recipient's locale, falling back to the default template

 

A few practical points:

  • Someone listed in both parameters receives two emails.
  • Use the internal-only parameter for employees and managers, so each person gets the template in their own language.
  • Keep shared mailboxes and distribution lists in the PMEmailRecipients picklist rather than typing addresses into the rule. A picklist change then needs no rule change.
  • Where I needed the email to reach the employee being reviewed, I added Form.Subject User in Get Users for Performance Management alongside the named HR users.

Testing tips and gotchas

  • Test by routing, not by saving. The rule fires only on Form Routing to Next Step. Saving the form, or submitting inside an iterative or collaboration step, does nothing.
  • Calibration doesn't trigger it. Saving ratings or routing forms inside a calibration session won't run Performance Management business rules.
  • Mobile isn't supported yet. SAP warns that mobile Performance Management doesn't support this scenario, so test carefully if your users route forms from the mobile app.
  • Existing forms are included. The rule applies to forms already in progress as well as new ones, so check open forms before you activate it in production.
  • Freeze the template. If you change a section or field the rule uses, review the rule again. If you rename the template, see the warning in step 1.
  • Check the placeholders. An unmapped placeholder or a custom token not linked in the rule leaves gaps in the email. Send a test to yourself first.
  • Mind the trigger limit. Each trigger accepts up to five rules per form template, so plan ahead if you also use other rule scenarios on routing.

Final thoughts

This scenario turns a Performance Management form into a trigger for follow-up actions, without custom code or manual monitoring. The setup takes some care: a picklist, a template group with mapped placeholders, a rule and an assignment. Once it's in place, the right people hear about the right outcomes at the moment the form moves on.

If you're already on the latest Performance Management form experience, this is one of the most practical 2H 2026 features to adopt.

Sources

  • New Rule Scenario: Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome (SAP release information)
  • Creating a Business Rule to Send Email Notifications Based on Assessment Outcome
  • Configuring Rule-Based Email Templates with Document Generation
  • Trigger Email Notification for Performance Management
  • Get Users for Performance Management
  • Assigning Business Rules for Performance Management

entry.title: Use SAP AI Core Models in VS Code Chat Without a Copilot Plan
entry.content:
VS Code’s Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) support lets developers use provider backed models in Chat without a Copilot plan. That can be useful when a team already has access to models through SAP AI Core and wants to work with them in VS Code.

There’s a small integration challenge with SAP AI Core service keys: they contain OAuth credentials and service URLs, not a standard model API key you can paste into a generic endpoint form. The client needs to exchange these credentials for an access token, then use that token and the correct resource group to make model requests.

I built SAPilot to handle those steps and make supported SAP AI Core deployments available in the VS Code Chat model picker.

What happens between Connect and Chat

After you enter your service key details, SAPilot stores the client secret in VS Code’s SecretStorage. The client ID, authentication URL, AI Core API URL, and resource group are stored separately as nonsecret connection settings. When SAPilot needs to call SAP AI Core, it requests an OAuth access token using the client credentials flow. The token is cached until shortly before it expires.

The exchange is the part that makes a service key different from a simple API key. This shortened example shows the same basic request SAPilot makes:

let tokenUrl = authUrl;
if (!tokenUrl.endsWith('/oauth/token')) tokenUrl += '/oauth/token';

const response = await fetch(`${tokenUrl}?grant_type=client_credentials`, {
  method: 'POST',
  redirect: 'error',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Basic ${Buffer.from(`${clientId}:${clientSecret}`).toString('base64')}`
  }
});

if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`SAP sign-in failed: ${response.status}`);
const { access_token: accessToken, expires_in: expiresIn } = await response.json();

For a chat request, SAPilot sends the access token as a bearer token and adds the AI-Resource-Group header. It also discovers running deployments and chooses a compatible request format for each supported chat model. This is why connecting SAP AI Core takes more than entering a base URL and a key.

A small security decision with a practical effect

A design choice was where to persist the values entered during setup. SAPilot uses VS Code’s SecretStorage for the client secret and globalState for the client ID and endpoint details. VS Code documents SecretStorage as encrypted storage for sensitive values, while extension state is intended for ordinary key-value data. Keeping the secret out of ordinary configuration avoids writing it alongside nonsecret settings.

This choice also affects setup: the secret is stored locally through VS Code and is not synced between machines, so you enter it again on another machine. SAPilot never needs a shared credential embedded in the extension; each developer connects using their own service key. Prompts and chat context are sent to the SAP AI Core model selected in Chat, so the model and service key should be chosen according to your organization’s data and access policies.

Why use the Chat Provider API?

VS Code’s Language Model Chat Provider API lets an extension contribute models to the existing picker and handle requests for them. SAPilot registers a provider, looks up deployments available to the connected service key, and returns the supported chat deployments to VS Code. When you select one, the extension translates the chat messages into that model’s request format and streams the response back into Chat.

That provider layer is useful here because SAP AI Core can expose different model families and request formats. SAPilot currently handles supported OpenAI compatible Chat Completions, Claude, Bedrock Converse, Cohere Chat, and Gemini on Vertex AI deployments. Deployments that are not supported chat models, such as embeddings, are left out of the picker.

The result is a familiar workflow: connect once, open Chat, and select an SAP AI Core deployment. You do not need to copy an access token into VS Code or manually add a resource-group header for every request.

Getting started and scope

Install SAPilot in VS Code 1.104 or later, run SAPilot: Connect to SAP AI Core, and enter your service key details. You need permission to use a running chat deployment. Then open Chat and select a model under SAP AI Core.

BYOK makes this chat workflow available without a Copilot plan, but model usage still follows the billing terms of your SAP AI Core account. Some VS Code capabilities, including inline suggestions and semantic search, remain tied to GitHub or Copilot services. Model cost, quality, and speed depend on the deployment, usage, and task.

A takeaway and what’s next

SAPilot shows how VS Code’s BYOK support can connect developers to models their organization already provides through SAP AI Core. BYOK changes which service handles chat requests; model usage still follows your SAP AI Core billing and your organization’s data policies. If you try SAPilot, have a question, or would like to suggest a feature, let me know in the comments. You can also contribute by raising a pull request on GitHub.

References

  • VS Code Language Model Chat Provider API
  • VS Code extension data storage and SecretStorage
  • SAP AI Core: Use a Service Key
  • SAPilot source code
